topics.name: Linux
topics.blurb: Boot, systemd, journalctl, df/du, memory, networking, performance

concepts.what: Firmware (BIOS/UEFI) → bootloader (GRUB) → kernel + initramfs → systemd starts as PID 1 → default target (multi-user or graphical) brings up services.
concepts.why: When a server won't come up, you fix it faster if you know which stage failed.
concepts.ex:
systemctl get-default        # which target it boots into
journalctl -xb                # logs from this boot
journalctl -b -1 -p err       # errors from the previous boot
systemctl rescue              # drop to rescue mode
concepts.tip: Stuck at GRUB = bootloader or disk problem. Boots but services are missing = a systemd unit problem.

concepts.what: systemd starts and supervises services defined in unit files. Your own units go in `/etc/systemd/system`.
concepts.why: Every 'service won't start' question is really a systemd question.
concepts.ex:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service
[Unit]
Description=My App
After=network.target

[Service]
User=app
ExecStart=/opt/myapp/run.sh
Restart=on-failure

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now myapp
systemctl status myapp
journalctl -u myapp -f
concepts.tip: `start` = run now. `enable` = run on boot. `enable --now` = both.

concepts.what: Disk → partition → LVM (physical volume → volume group → logical volume) → filesystem (xfs/ext4) → mount point.
concepts.why: 'Disk full' and 'extend the disk' are the two most common infra tickets.
concepts.ex:
df -h                               # which filesystem is full
du -xsh /var/* | sort -h | tail     # what's using it
lsof +L1                            # deleted files still held open
> /var/log/app.log                  # truncate a log safely

# grow a VM disk on LVM, no reboot
growpart /dev/sda 2
pvresize /dev/sda2
lvextend -r -l +100%FREE /dev/mapper/vg-root
concepts.tip: `-r` on lvextend grows the filesystem in the same step.

concepts.what: Read/write/execute for owner, group and others. Numbers: r=4, w=2, x=1, so 7=rwx, 6=rw, 5=rx, 4=r.
concepts.why: 'App can't read its config' is usually ownership or mode.
concepts.ex:
ls -l config.yml
-rw------- 1 root root config.yml   # app user can't read it

chown app:app config.yml
chmod 640 config.yml
id app                              # which groups the user is in
sudo -l -U app                      # what sudo allows
concepts.tip: 755 for scripts and folders, 644 for files, 600 for private keys.

concepts.what: Load average = processes running or waiting on disk, averaged over 1, 5 and 15 minutes. Compare it to the CPU core count.
concepts.why: 'Server is slow' questions test whether you can tell CPU, memory and disk problems apart.
concepts.ex:
uptime                 # load 12 on 4 cores = overloaded
nproc                  # core count
top                    # high 'wa' = waiting on disk
iostat -x 1            # %util near 100 = disk bottleneck
free -m
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head
kill -15 <pid>         # graceful stop
kill -9 <pid>          # force, last resort
concepts.tip: High load with low CPU almost always means I/O wait.

concepts.what: Walk the layers bottom-up: interface → gateway → DNS → remote port → local listener → firewall → packets.
concepts.why: Interviewers want a method, not random commands.
concepts.ex:
ip a                      # 1. interface up, has an IP?
ip r                      # 2. default gateway
ping <gateway>
dig app.example.com       # 3. does DNS resolve?
nc -zv db01 5432          # 4. is the remote port open?
ss -tlnp                  # 5. is my app listening (0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1)?
firewall-cmd --list-all   # 6. local firewall
tcpdump -i eth0 port 443  # 7. look at the actual packets
concepts.tip: Ping works but the port times out = firewall, not routing.

concepts.what: System logs live in the journal and `/var/log`. logrotate keeps them from filling the disk.
concepts.why: Logs are your first stop in every incident.
concepts.ex:
journalctl --since "1 hour ago" -p err
tail -f /var/log/messages      # RHEL
tail -f /var/log/syslog        # Ubuntu
dmesg -T | grep -i oom         # kernel killed something?

# /etc/logrotate.d/myapp
/var/log/myapp/*.log {
  daily
  rotate 7
  compress
  missingok
}
concepts.tip: Fix the cause (logrotate, log level), not just today's full disk.

concepts.what: Key-based login: private key stays with you, public key goes in the server's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`.
concepts.why: You'll be asked how you secure and debug remote access.
concepts.ex:
ssh-keygen -t ed25519
ssh-copy-id user@host
chmod 700 ~/.ssh
chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
ssh -vvv user@host            # shows where login fails

# /etc/ssh/sshd_config
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
concepts.tip: Wrong permissions on `.ssh` silently break key login.

concepts.what: Extra access control on top of normal permissions (RHEL). Files and ports carry labels; a mismatch is denied even if chmod looks right.
concepts.why: Classic trick question: 'permissions are 755 but nginx still gets 403'.
concepts.ex:
getenforce
ausearch -m avc -ts recent          # what was denied
restorecon -Rv /data/www            # fix file labels
semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 8081
setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on
concepts.tip: Never answer 'disable SELinux'. Read the denial and fix the label.

concepts.what: RHEL uses dnf/yum, Ubuntu uses apt. Patch non-prod first, then prod in waves inside a change window.
concepts.why: Patching is half of infra operations, and it's daily work in most infra roles.
concepts.ex:
# RHEL
dnf check-update
dnf update -y
dnf history
dnf history undo <id>
needs-restarting -r                 # reboot needed?

# Ubuntu
apt update && apt upgrade -y
ls /var/run/reboot-required
concepts.tip: `apt update` refreshes the list; `apt upgrade` installs. You need both.

concepts.what: systemd-journald collects kernel messages, boot messages, service stdout/stderr and syslog into one indexed binary journal. `journalctl` queries it by unit, time, boot, priority or PID. Priorities: 0 emerg, 1 alert, 2 crit, 3 err, 4 warning, 5 notice, 6 info, 7 debug.
concepts.why: On any modern distro (RHEL 7+, Ubuntu 16.04+) this is the first place you look when a service fails or a box rebooted. If you can't filter the journal fast, you look slow in a live troubleshooting round.
concepts.ex:
journalctl -u nginx -f                    # follow one service live
journalctl -u nginx --since "10 min ago"
journalctl -u nginx --since "2026-11-16 02:00" --until "2026-11-16 02:30"
journalctl -p err -b                      # errors, this boot
journalctl -b -1 -e                       # end of PREVIOUS boot (why did it die?)
journalctl --list-boots                   # boot history
journalctl -k                             # kernel only (like dmesg)
journalctl _PID=1234                      # one process
journalctl -u myapp -o json-pretty -n 5   # see all fields
journalctl -u myapp --no-pager | grep -i timeout

journalctl --disk-usage
journalctl --vacuum-time=7d               # trim old entries
journalctl --vacuum-size=500M

# make it survive reboots
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf -> Storage=persistent, SystemMaxUse=1G
mkdir -p /var/log/journal && systemctl restart systemd-journald
concepts.tip: Previous-boot logs only exist if the journal is persistent. Check `Storage=` in journald.conf and whether `/var/log/journal` exists. Say this when asked 'why can't you see logs from before the crash?'

concepts.what: `df` asks each mounted filesystem how much is used and free. `du` walks directories and adds up file sizes. `-h` = human-readable (K/M/G). They disagree when a deleted file is still open, when files are hidden under a mount point, or because ext4 reserves ~5% for root. (There's no `dh` command; people usually mean `df -h`.)
concepts.why: 'Disk full' is the number-one Linux ticket, and 'df and du don't match' is the number-one follow-up question.
concepts.ex:
df -hT                               # size/used/avail + filesystem type
df -i                                # INODES. 100% IUse% = 'No space left' even with free GB
du -sh /var/log                      # total for one folder
du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h     # -x = don't cross into other mounts
ncdu -x /                            # interactive, if installed
find / -xdev -type f -size +1G -exec ls -lh {} \;
lsof +L1                             # deleted but still open: df counts it, du can't see it

# files hidden under a mount point
mount --bind / /mnt/rootonly && du -sh /mnt/rootonly/data

tune2fs -l /dev/sda1 | grep -i 'reserved block'   # ext4 root reserve
concepts.tip: 'No space left on device' with free GB = inodes. Usually millions of tiny files (session files, mail queue, cache). Find them with `find /path -xdev -type f | cut -d/ -f2-3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -n | tail`.

concepts.what: Linux uses spare RAM as page cache, so `free` looks low on a healthy box. The number that matters is `available`. Swap activity (pages moving in and out), not swap size, signals real pressure.
concepts.why: Saying 'the server is out of memory because free is 200 MB' is an instant junior signal.
concepts.ex:
free -h
#        total  used  free   buff/cache  available
# Mem:    15Gi  4.1Gi 210Mi  11Gi        10Gi     <- healthy

vmstat 1 5          # si/so non-zero every second = actively swapping = real pressure
swapon --show
cat /proc/meminfo | egrep 'MemAvailable|Dirty|Slab'
ps aux --sort=-rss | head          # biggest resident processes
sysctl vm.swappiness               # 60 default; DB servers often 1-10
dmesg -T | grep -i -E 'oom|killed process'
concepts.tip: Free is low but available is high = normal. Available low + swap in/out + OOM kills = real problem.

concepts.what: The modern commands (iproute2, ss, dig, curl) plus the files that control name resolution: `/etc/hosts`, `/etc/resolv.conf`, `/etc/nsswitch.conf`.
concepts.why: Every infra interview has a 'can't connect' question. Knowing which tool answers which layer is the whole game.
concepts.ex:
ip -br a                         # interfaces + IPs, one line each
ip r ; ip route get 10.2.0.11    # which route + interface a packet will use
ip neigh                         # ARP table (L2 neighbours)
ip -s link show eth0             # RX/TX errors and drops
ethtool eth0                     # link speed, duplex
ss -tulnp                        # listening TCP/UDP + owning process
ss -tan state established | wc -l
ss -ti dst 10.2.0.11             # per-connection RTT, retransmits, cwnd

cat /etc/resolv.conf             # which DNS servers
getent hosts app.example.com     # resolves the SAME way the app does (hosts file + DNS)
dig +short app.example.com

curl -vk https://app.example.com/health
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns:%{time_namelookup} tcp:%{time_connect} tls:%{time_appconnect} ttfb:%{time_starttransfer} total:%{time_total}\n' https://app.example.com
nc -zv db01 5432
traceroute -T -p 443 app.example.com   # TCP traceroute gets past ICMP blocks
mtr -rwc 100 app.example.com           # loss + latency per hop
tcpdump -nni any host 10.2.0.11 and port 443 -w /tmp/cap.pcap
nmcli con show                          # NetworkManager (RHEL)

# old -> new:  ifconfig -> ip a   netstat -tlnp -> ss -tlnp   route -n -> ip r
concepts.tip: `dig` ignores `/etc/hosts`; the app doesn't. Use `getent hosts` to see what the app actually resolves.

concepts.t: Text processing: grep, awk, sed, find
concepts.what: Most log analysis and quick automation is a pipeline of small tools.
concepts.why: Live rounds often say 'here's an access log, give me the top 10 client IPs'. You need to type it, not describe it.
concepts.ex:
grep -rin "error" /var/log/myapp/
grep -c ' 500 ' access.log                 # count 500s
grep -v '^#' app.conf | grep -v '^$'       # config without comments/blanks

awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head    # top client IPs
awk '{print $9}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn           # status code counts
awk -F: '$3 >= 1000 {print $1}' /etc/passwd                       # real users

sed -i.bak 's/timeout=30/timeout=60/' app.conf    # edit in place, keep backup
sed -n '100,120p' big.log                         # print lines 100-120

find /var/log -name '*.log' -mtime +30 -delete
find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null      # SUID binaries (security)
tail -f app.log | grep --line-buffered ERROR
cut -d, -f2 data.csv | sort -u
concepts.tip: Practice the `awk | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head` pipeline until you can type it without thinking.

concepts.what: Accounts live in `/etc/passwd`, password hashes in `/etc/shadow` (root-only), groups in `/etc/group`. sudo rules live in `/etc/sudoers` and `/etc/sudoers.d/`, edited only with `visudo`.
concepts.why: Access requests and 'user can't log in' tickets are daily work, and least privilege is a security question.
concepts.ex:
useradd -m -s /bin/bash jdoe
passwd jdoe
chage -l jdoe                    # password expiry info
usermod -aG docker jdoe          # -a = APPEND. Without it you remove other groups
id jdoe ; getent passwd jdoe
last -n 10 ; lastb               # successful / failed logins

visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/myapp
# allow one command only
app ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart myapp

# AD-joined Linux (sssd / realmd)
realm list
id jdoe@corp.local
concepts.tip: `usermod -G` without `-a` silently removes the user from every other group. Real outages have come from that one letter.

concepts.what: cron runs commands on a schedule: minute, hour, day-of-month, month, day-of-week. systemd timers do the same with logging and dependencies.
concepts.why: 'The job works when I run it, but not from cron' is a classic.
concepts.ex:
crontab -e                        # current user
crontab -l -u app
# m  h  dom mon dow  command
*/5  *  *   *   *    /opt/scripts/check.sh >> /var/log/check.log 2>&1
0    2  *   *   0    /opt/scripts/weekly.sh

ls /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.daily
systemctl list-timers
grep CRON /var/log/cron           # RHEL
journalctl -u cron                # Ubuntu
concepts.tip: Works by hand but not in cron = environment. cron has a tiny PATH, no profile, maybe a different user. Use full paths and log stdout+stderr.

concepts.what: `/etc` config, `/var` changing data and logs, `/opt` third-party apps, `/home` users, `/tmp` scratch, `/boot` kernel, `/proc` and `/sys` live kernel info. `/etc/fstab` lists what mounts at boot.
concepts.why: A bad fstab line drops a server into emergency mode on reboot, which is a bad way to find out.
concepts.ex:
lsblk -f                          # disks, partitions, filesystems, UUIDs
blkid
findmnt                           # what's mounted where

# /etc/fstab
UUID=3f1c...  /data        xfs  defaults,nofail      0 0
nas01:/export /mnt/share   nfs  defaults,_netdev     0 0

mount -a                          # test fstab BEFORE rebooting
findmnt --verify
showmount -e nas01                # what an NFS server exports

/proc/cpuinfo  /proc/meminfo  /proc/<pid>/   # live kernel data
concepts.tip: Always run `mount -a` after editing fstab. Use UUIDs, not /dev/sdX, and `nofail` / `_netdev` for non-critical or network mounts.

concepts.what: USE method: for each resource (CPU, memory, disk, network) check Utilization, Saturation and Errors. Brendan Gregg's 60-second list covers it.
concepts.why: 'Server is slow' is the most common senior Linux question. A fixed order sounds senior; random commands don't.
concepts.ex:
uptime                    # load trend (1/5/15 min)
dmesg -T | tail           # OOM, disk or NIC errors
vmstat 1                  # r = run queue, b = blocked on IO, si/so = swap, wa = IO wait
mpstat -P ALL 1           # one core at 100% = single-threaded bottleneck
pidstat 1                 # CPU per process
iostat -xz 1              # %util, await (ms per IO), r/s w/s per disk
free -m
sar -n DEV 1              # network throughput per NIC
sar -n TCP,ETCP 1         # retransmits
top / htop

# deeper
pidstat -d 1              # which process does the IO
strace -f -tt -p <pid>    # what syscall is it stuck on
lsof -p <pid> | wc -l     # open files vs ulimit
sar -u -f /var/log/sa/sa15   # yesterday's CPU (sysstat history)
concepts.tip: Name the method: 'I use the USE method, starting with uptime, dmesg, vmstat, iostat.' Then go where the numbers point.

concepts.what: States: R running, S sleeping, D uninterruptible (waiting on IO), Z zombie, T stopped. Signals: 15 TERM (ask nicely), 9 KILL (can't be caught), 1 HUP (often reload config), 2 INT (Ctrl+C).
concepts.why: 'kill -9 doesn't work' and 'too many open files' both come up.
concepts.ex:
ps -ef --forest ; pstree -p
ps -eo pid,stat,cmd | awk '$2 ~ /D/'     # stuck in IO
pgrep -a java ; pkill -f 'myapp.jar'
nice -n 10 ./batch.sh ; renice 5 -p <pid>
nohup ./long.sh > out.log 2>&1 &

ulimit -n                                # open-files limit for this shell
cat /proc/<pid>/limits                   # the REAL limits of a running process
# systemd service: set in the unit, limits.conf doesn't apply
[Service]
LimitNOFILE=65536
concepts.tip: A process in D state ignores kill -9 because it's waiting in the kernel, usually on hung NFS or a failing disk. Fix the storage, not the process.

concepts.t: Logging stack: journald, rsyslog, central logs
concepts.what: journald captures logs; rsyslog writes the classic text files and can forward to a central system (Splunk, ELK, Loki, Azure Monitor). Key files: `/var/log/messages` or `syslog`, `/var/log/secure` or `auth.log`, `/var/log/cron`, `/var/log/audit/audit.log`.
concepts.why: Centralized logging is a standard design question: 'how do you get logs from 500 servers and why bother?'
concepts.ex:
# /etc/rsyslog.d/50-forward.conf
*.*  @@logserver.corp.local:514     # @@ = TCP, @ = UDP
systemctl restart rsyslog
logger -p user.err "test from $(hostname)"   # prove forwarding works

# where auth events go
/var/log/secure      (RHEL)
/var/log/auth.log    (Ubuntu)

# app logs: file + logrotate, or stdout in containers
# good logs: timestamp (UTC), level, request/correlation ID, JSON
concepts.tip: Why central logs: the server may be dead or rebuilt, an attacker can wipe local logs, and you need to search 50 servers at once.

qa.q: Walk me through the Linux boot process.
qa.a: Firmware runs POST and hands off to GRUB. GRUB loads the kernel and initramfs. The kernel starts the hardware, mounts the real root filesystem and launches systemd as PID 1. systemd brings up the default target and its services.

qa.q: A disk is 100% full. What do you do?
qa.a: `df -h` to find the filesystem, then `du -xsh /path/* | sort -h` to find the biggest folder. It's usually logs: truncate or compress them, then fix logrotate so it doesn't come back. If `du` doesn't add up, a deleted file is still open. Find it with `lsof +L1` and restart that process.

qa.q: Difference between systemctl start and enable?
qa.a: `start` runs the service now. `enable` makes it start at boot. `enable --now` does both.

qa.q: What does chmod 755 mean?
qa.a: Owner can read, write and execute. Group and others can read and execute. It's the normal mode for scripts and directories.

qa.q: Difference between su and sudo?
qa.a: `su` switches to another user and needs that user's password. `sudo` runs one command as root with your own password, is logged, and can be limited per command in sudoers.

qa.q: Load is high but CPU usage is low. What's happening?
qa.a: Processes are waiting on I/O, usually disk, not computing. Check `top` for high `wa`, run `iostat -x 1` for a busy device, and look for processes in D state.

qa.q: What is a zombie process?
qa.a: A finished process whose parent hasn't collected its exit status. It uses no CPU or memory. You fix the parent (restart or signal it), not the zombie.

qa.q: The app works on port 8080 locally but not from other servers. Why?
qa.a: Check `ss -tlnp`. If it's bound to 127.0.0.1, it only accepts local connections; rebind to 0.0.0.0. Then check the local firewall and any network firewall between the servers.

qa.q: SSH says Permission denied (publickey). What do you check?
qa.a: Right user? Key in `authorized_keys`? Permissions 700 on `.ssh` and 600 on the key file? Key auth disabled in sshd_config? SELinux context on `.ssh`? `ssh -vvv` shows which step fails.

qa.q: What is the OOM killer?
qa.a: When memory runs out, the kernel kills the process with the highest OOM score. Confirm with `dmesg -T | grep -i oom`. Fix by right-sizing, setting memory limits, or fixing the leak.

qa.q: How do you add 20 GB to a VM's root filesystem?
qa.a: Grow the disk in VMware, rescan it, `growpart` the partition, `pvresize` the physical volume, then `lvextend -r` to grow the logical volume and filesystem together. No reboot.

qa.q: The app works with SELinux permissive but fails in enforcing. Fix?
qa.a: Don't disable SELinux. Read the denial with `ausearch -m avc`, then fix the file label with `restorecon`, add a port label with `semanage port`, or turn on the right boolean.

qa.q: How would you patch 150 Linux machines safely?
qa.a: Test the patch set on non-prod first. Snapshot or back up. Patch in waves inside a change window, using automation like Ansible so every box gets the same thing. Check service health after each wave before starting the next. Keep a rollback ready (snapshot revert or `dnf history undo`) and report compliance at the end.

qa.q: How do you see the last hour of logs for one service, and follow it live?
qa.a: `journalctl -u <service> --since "1 hour ago"`, and `journalctl -u <service> -f` to follow. Add `-p err` for errors only, `-b` for this boot, `-b -1` for the previous boot.

qa.q: df vs du?
qa.a: `df` reports used and free space per mounted filesystem, from the filesystem's own accounting. `du` adds up the sizes of files it can walk to. `-h` makes both human-readable. Use `df -h` to find which mount is full, then `du -xh --max-depth=1 <mount> | sort -h` to find what's filling it.

qa.q: How do you find which process is listening on port 8080?
qa.a: `ss -tlnp | grep 8080` (or `lsof -i :8080`). It shows the process, PID and bind address. If it's bound to 127.0.0.1, only local clients can reach it.

qa.q: What's the difference between /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow?
qa.a: `/etc/passwd` is world-readable and holds username, UID, GID, home directory and shell. `/etc/shadow` is readable only by root and holds the password hashes and expiry settings.

qa.q: Hard link vs symbolic link?
qa.a: A hard link is another name for the same inode: same data, survives deleting the original, can't cross filesystems or point at directories. A symlink is a small file containing a path: can cross filesystems, but breaks if the target moves.

qa.q: What does `> file 2>&1` mean?
qa.a: Send stdout (1) to the file, then send stderr (2) to wherever stdout is going, so both end up in the file. Order matters: `2>&1 > file` sends stderr to the terminal.

qa.q: How do you find files larger than 1 GB?
qa.a: `find / -xdev -type f -size +1G -exec ls -lh {} \;`. `-xdev` keeps it on one filesystem so it doesn't crawl NFS mounts or /proc.

qa.q: df says the disk is 100% full but du only adds up to 60%. Why?
qa.a: Most often a deleted file still held open by a process (a log deleted instead of truncated). Find it with `lsof +L1` and restart or signal that process. Other causes: files hidden underneath a mount point (bind-mount / to check), or ext4's ~5% root reserve.

qa.q: 'No space left on device' but df -h shows 40% free. Why?
qa.a: Out of inodes. Check `df -i`. Usually millions of tiny files: PHP sessions, a mail queue, a cache folder. Find the directory with the most files and clean it up, then fix whatever is creating them.

qa.q: free shows 200 MB free on a 16 GB server. Is that a problem?
qa.a: Not by itself. Linux uses spare RAM for page cache. Look at the `available` column and at swap activity in `vmstat 1` (si/so). If available is several GB and nothing is swapping, it's healthy. Low available plus swapping or OOM kills is a real problem.

qa.q: The server rebooted overnight. How do you find out why on Linux?
qa.a: `last -x reboot shutdown` for the times, `journalctl --list-boots` and `journalctl -b -1 -e` for the last messages before it went down (needs a persistent journal), `/var/log/messages` or `syslog`, `dmesg` for kernel panics, `/var/crash` if kdump is set up. Also check the hypervisor or cloud side: vCenter events, Azure Activity Log and Resource Health for host maintenance.

qa.q: journalctl shows nothing from before the reboot. Why?
qa.a: The journal is volatile: stored in `/run/log/journal` (RAM). Set `Storage=persistent` in `/etc/systemd/journald.conf` or create `/var/log/journal`, then restart systemd-journald. Cap it with `SystemMaxUse`.

qa.q: A script works when you run it but fails from cron. Why?
qa.a: Different environment: cron has a minimal PATH, doesn't load your profile, may run as a different user and has no terminal. Use absolute paths, set variables in the script, and redirect output (`>> log 2>&1`) so you can see the error.

qa.q: An app logs 'Too many open files'. Fix?
qa.a: Check the real limit with `cat /proc/<pid>/limits` and current usage with `ls /proc/<pid>/fd | wc -l`. For a systemd service raise `LimitNOFILE` in the unit (limits.conf doesn't apply to services), daemon-reload and restart. Also check for a descriptor leak if it keeps climbing.

qa.q: How do you prove whether DNS is the problem for an app?
qa.a: Check `/etc/resolv.conf`, then `getent hosts <name>` (resolves the same way the app does, including /etc/hosts) and `dig <name>` against each DNS server. Compare to a known-good host. Time it: slow lookups show up in `curl -w '%{time_namelookup}'`.

qa.q: Give the one-liner for the top 10 client IPs in an Nginx access log.
qa.a: `awk '{print $1}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head`. Swap `$1` for `$9` to count status codes.

qa.q: What's the risk with /etc/fstab and how do you avoid it?
qa.a: A wrong line (bad UUID, missing NFS server) can stop the boot in emergency mode. Use UUIDs, add `nofail` for non-critical mounts and `_netdev` for network mounts, and always run `mount -a` or `findmnt --verify` before rebooting.

qa.q: How do you find which process is causing heavy disk I/O?
qa.a: `iostat -xz 1` to confirm which device is busy (%util, await), then `pidstat -d 1` or `iotop` to see which process is reading or writing.

qa.q: Should production servers have swap? What is swappiness?
qa.a: A small amount of swap is a safety net that buys time before the OOM killer. Swappiness (default 60) controls how eagerly the kernel swaps; database servers often set it to 1-10. Constant swapping in `vmstat` means you need more RAM or a smaller workload, not more swap.

qa.q: A Linux server is 'slow'. Walk me through your first 60 seconds.
qa.a: Clarify: slow for whom, since when, what changed. Then the USE checklist: `uptime` (load trend), `dmesg -T | tail` (OOM, disk errors), `vmstat 1` (run queue, IO wait, swap), `mpstat -P ALL 1` (one core pegged?), `iostat -xz 1` (disk latency), `free -m`, `sar -n DEV 1` and `sar -n TCP,ETCP 1` (network and retransmits), then `top` or `pidstat` for the process. Follow the numbers, and check whether it's the server at all or a dependency like the database.

qa.q: A process is stuck in D state and kill -9 doesn't work. What's going on?
qa.a: It's in uninterruptible sleep inside the kernel, waiting on IO, typically a hung NFS mount or a failing disk or SAN path. Signals are only delivered when it returns. Check `dmesg` for IO or NFS errors, fix the storage path (or force-unmount NFS with `umount -f -l`); a reboot may be the only option if the device is gone.

qa.q: How would you get logs from 500 servers into one place, and why?
qa.a: Agent on every host (rsyslog/Fluent Bit/Filebeat, or Azure Monitor Agent) shipping to a central store (Splunk, ELK, Loki, Log Analytics), deployed with Ansible or a golden image. Structured JSON, consistent timestamps in UTC, retention by type, access control. Why: servers die or get rebuilt, attackers wipe local logs, and incidents need correlation across many hosts.

topics.name: Scripting & Automation
topics.blurb: Bash, PowerShell, Python and jq for live exercises and fleet work

concepts.what: Shebang, safe mode, variables (always quote them), conditionals, loops, functions, exit codes. `$?` is the last command's exit code; 0 = success.
concepts.why: Many infra rounds include a short live scripting task. Syntax hesitation reads as 'doesn't actually script'.
concepts.ex:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail          # stop on error, unset var, failed pipe

LOG=/var/log/check.log
THRESHOLD=${1:-90}         # first argument, default 90

log() { echo "$(date -Is) $*" | tee -a "$LOG"; }

if [[ $(id -u) -ne 0 ]]; then
  echo "run as root" >&2; exit 1
fi

for svc in nginx sshd chronyd; do
  if systemctl is-active --quiet "$svc"; then
    log "OK   $svc"
  else
    log "DOWN $svc"
  fi
done
concepts.tip: Quote every variable: `"$var"`. Unquoted variables break on spaces and empty values and are the #1 bash bug.

concepts.what: A classic take-home or live task: check every filesystem and report anything over a threshold.
concepts.why: Shows parsing, loops, thresholds and exit codes in one small script.
concepts.ex:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
THRESHOLD=${1:-85}
rc=0
# -P = POSIX one-line output; skip tmpfs/devtmpfs
while read -r fs size used avail pct mount; do
  p=${pct%\%}
  if (( p >= THRESHOLD )); then
    echo "WARN $mount at ${p}% ($avail free)"
    rc=1
  fi
done < <(df -P -h -x tmpfs -x devtmpfs | tail -n +2)
exit $rc       # non-zero lets cron/monitoring detect it
concepts.tip: Returning a non-zero exit code makes the script usable by monitoring, cron alerts and pipelines.

concepts.t: Script: run checks across many hosts
concepts.what: Loop over a host list with SSH, or test ports in parallel. For real fleets, use Ansible.
concepts.why: 'How would you check X on 200 servers?' always comes up.
concepts.ex:
# port check, 20 at a time
cat hosts.txt | xargs -P 20 -I{} sh -c 'nc -z -w 3 {} 443 && echo "OK {}" || echo "FAIL {}"'

# run a command over SSH (BatchMode = don't hang on password prompts)
while read -r h; do
  out=$(ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5 "$h" 'uptime -p; df -h / | tail -1' 2>&1) \
    && echo "$h: $out" || echo "$h: UNREACHABLE"
done < hosts.txt

# the right tool at scale
ansible all -i inventory -m shell -a 'df -h /' -f 30
ansible web -i inventory -m service -a 'name=nginx state=restarted' --become
concepts.tip: `ssh` inside a `while read` loop eats stdin; use `ssh -n` or read from a different file descriptor if the loop stops after one host.

concepts.what: Objects, not text: filter with Where-Object, pick with Select-Object, export with Export-Csv. Remote with Invoke-Command (WinRM).
concepts.why: Windows-heavy shops will ask for PowerShell, not bash.
concepts.tip: Use `Get-CimInstance`, not the old `Get-WmiObject` (removed in PowerShell 7).

concepts.what: Use Python when bash gets messy: APIs, JSON, retries, real error handling, anything over ~50 lines.
concepts.why: Many teams now expect basic Python for automation and API calls.
concepts.ex:
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import sys, time, requests

URLS = ["https://app.example.com/health", "https://api.example.com/health"]
failed = 0
for url in URLS:
    start = time.monotonic()
    try:
        r = requests.get(url, timeout=5)
        ms = (time.monotonic() - start) * 1000
        status = "OK" if r.status_code == 200 else "BAD"
        print(f"{status} {url} {r.status_code} {ms:.0f}ms")
        failed += status != "OK"
    except requests.RequestException as e:
        print(f"FAIL {url} {e}")
        failed += 1
sys.exit(1 if failed else 0)
concepts.tip: Rule of thumb: bash to glue commands, Python for logic, APIs and JSON, Ansible for fleets, Terraform for cloud resources.

concepts.t: JSON on the command line: jq and az --query
concepts.what: Cloud CLIs and APIs return JSON. `jq` filters it; `az ... --query` uses JMESPath.
concepts.why: You'll pipe cloud output into scripts constantly.
concepts.ex:
# jq
curl -s https://api.example.com/items | jq '.items[] | {name, status}'
kubectl get pods -o json | jq -r '.items[] | select(.status.phase!="Running") | .metadata.name'

# az --query (JMESPath)
az vm list -d --query "[?powerState!='VM running'].{name:name, rg:resourceGroup}" -o table
az network nsg rule list -g rg --nsg-name nsg-web \
  --query "[?access=='Allow' && direction=='Inbound'].{n:name,p:priority,port:destinationPortRange}" -o table
concepts.tip: `-o tsv` gives raw values for use in bash variables: `ip=$(az vm show -d -g rg -n vm1 --query privateIps -o tsv)`.

concepts.t: Writing scripts that are safe in prod
concepts.what: Idempotent, logged, dry-run capable, fail loudly, no secrets inside, version-controlled, reviewed.
concepts.why: Seniors are asked 'how do you make sure your script doesn't take down prod?'
concepts.ex:
[ ] set -euo pipefail (bash) / $ErrorActionPreference='Stop' (PS)
[ ] --dry-run flag that prints what it WOULD do
[ ] check before change (idempotent): only act if not already correct
[ ] log what you did, to a file and stdout, with timestamps
[ ] limit blast radius: run on 1 host, then 10%, then all
[ ] timeouts on network calls
[ ] secrets from a vault / env, never hard-coded
[ ] in Git, reviewed via pull request
[ ] tested with shellcheck / PSScriptAnalyzer
concepts.tip: `shellcheck script.sh` catches most bash bugs before they hit prod. Mention it.

qa.q: What does set -euo pipefail do?
qa.a: `-e` exits when a command fails, `-u` errors on unset variables, `-o pipefail` makes a pipeline fail if any command in it fails, not just the last. Together they stop scripts from blindly continuing after an error.

qa.q: What does $? hold?
qa.a: The exit code of the last command: 0 for success, non-zero for failure. Scripts and monitoring use it to decide what happened.

qa.q: Single vs double quotes in bash?
qa.a: Single quotes are literal: no variable or command expansion. Double quotes expand `$var` and `$(cmd)` but keep spaces intact. Use double quotes around variables almost always.

qa.q: How do you pass arguments to a bash script?
qa.a: `$1`, `$2`... for positional args, `$@` for all of them (quoted: `"$@"`), `$#` for the count, and `${1:-default}` for a default value.

qa.q: Write a script that restarts a service if it isn't running.
qa.a: `if ! systemctl is-active --quiet nginx; then systemctl restart nginx; logger "nginx restarted by watchdog"; fi`. Then mention that systemd's `Restart=on-failure` usually makes this unnecessary, and that you'd alert rather than silently restart forever.

qa.q: How do you run a command on 100 servers?
qa.a: Ansible ad-hoc or a playbook (`ansible all -m shell -a 'cmd' -f 30`) for Linux, `Invoke-Command -ComputerName` for Windows. A bash loop with `ssh -o BatchMode=yes -o ConnectTimeout=5` works in a pinch. Always test on one host first, then a small batch.

qa.q: PowerShell passes objects; bash passes text. Why does that matter?
qa.a: In PowerShell you filter and select properties directly (`Where-Object Status -eq 'Running'`) without parsing columns. In bash you parse text with awk/cut, which breaks if output format changes. Objects make scripts more reliable and easy to export (CSV, JSON).

qa.q: How do you parse JSON in a shell script?
qa.a: `jq`: e.g. `jq -r '.items[].name'`. For Azure CLI use `--query` with JMESPath and `-o tsv` for raw values. Don't grep JSON.

qa.q: When do you use bash vs Python vs Ansible?
qa.a: Bash for short glue around Linux commands. Python when there's logic, JSON/APIs, retries or it's growing past ~50 lines. Ansible when the job is 'make many servers look like this' and needs idempotency and inventory.

qa.q: How do you make sure your automation can't take down production?
qa.a: Idempotent checks before changes, a dry-run mode, strict error handling, timeouts, secrets from a vault, code review in Git, linting (shellcheck), and a staged rollout: one host, a canary group, then the rest, with a health check gate between stages and a documented rollback.

topics.name: Windows Server
topics.blurb: AD, Group Policy, DNS, PowerShell, event IDs

concepts.what: Directory of users, computers and groups. Domain controllers (DCs) authenticate logins and replicate changes to each other.
concepts.why: Logins, permissions and policy all run through AD.
concepts.ex:
Search-ADAccount -LockedOut
Unlock-ADAccount jdoe
Get-ADUser jdoe -Properties LockedOut,PasswordExpired
Get-ADGroupMember "App-Admins"
Test-ComputerSecureChannel -Repair   # fix broken domain trust
concepts.tip: Always run at least two DCs per domain.

concepts.what: Central settings pushed to users and computers. Applied in order Local → Site → Domain → OU; the last one wins.
concepts.why: 'Setting isn't applying' is a classic Windows question.
concepts.ex:
gpresult /r          # which GPOs applied
gpupdate /force
rsop.msc             # resultant set of policy
concepts.tip: GPOs link to OUs, not to groups. Groups are only used for filtering.

concepts.what: AD depends on DNS: DCs register SRV records so clients can find them. DHCP hands out IPs from scopes.
concepts.why: Half of 'AD is broken' tickets are really DNS.
concepts.ex:
nslookup app.corp.local
nslookup -type=SRV _ldap._tcp.dc._msdcs.corp.local
ipconfig /all
ipconfig /flushdns
ipconfig /registerdns
concepts.tip: If the SRV lookup comes back empty, fix DNS before touching AD.

concepts.what: The admin shell for Windows. Commands are Verb-Noun and pass objects, not text.
concepts.why: Interviewers ask you to show you can work without the GUI.
concepts.ex:
Get-Service | Where Status -eq 'Stopped'
Restart-Service Spooler
Get-Process | Sort CPU -Desc | Select -First 5
Test-NetConnection db01 -Port 1433
Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
Get-HotFix | Sort InstalledOn -Desc
Get-Volume
concepts.tip: `Test-NetConnection` is the Windows version of `nc -zv`.

concepts.what: Event Viewer logs everything. A few IDs come up again and again.
concepts.why: 'Why did the server reboot?' is answered from these.
concepts.ex:
4624  successful logon
4625  failed logon
4740  account locked out
1074  planned restart (shows who or what)
6008  unexpected shutdown
41    Kernel-Power (crash or power loss)
7034  service crashed

Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='System'; Id=1074} -MaxEvents 5
concepts.tip: 1074 = someone or something asked for it. 6008 or 41 = it crashed.

concepts.what: A shared folder has share permissions and NTFS permissions. The effective access is the most restrictive of the two.
concepts.why: 'Full Control but can't write' is a favorite trick question.
concepts.ex:
Get-SmbShareAccess -Name Finance
Get-Acl D:\Finance | Format-List
# GUI: folder → Properties → Security → Advanced → Effective Access
concepts.tip: Common practice: share = Everyone Full Control, control access with NTFS.

concepts.what: WSUS, SCCM/MECM or Intune approve updates and push them in rings. Patch Tuesday is the second Tuesday of the month.
concepts.why: You'll be asked how you patch and how you roll back.
concepts.ex:
Get-HotFix -Id KB5034441
wusa /uninstall /kb:5034441 /quiet /norestart
# reboot pending?
Test-Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\WindowsUpdate\Auto Update\RebootRequired'
concepts.tip: After uninstalling a bad patch, decline it in WSUS or it comes right back.

concepts.what: The Windows equivalents of the Linux commands you already know.
concepts.why: Many infra roles are mixed estates. Panels check you're not lost on the other OS.
concepts.ex:
Linux            Windows
ip a             ipconfig /all ; Get-NetIPAddress
ip r             route print ; Get-NetRoute
ss -tlnp         netstat -ano | findstr LISTENING ; Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
nc -zv h 443     Test-NetConnection h -Port 443
dig              Resolve-DnsName app.corp.local
traceroute       tracert ; pathping (adds loss per hop)
tcpdump          pktmon / netsh trace start capture=yes ; Wireshark
top              Task Manager, Resource Monitor (resmon)
iostat/vmstat    perfmon: % Processor Time, Avg. Disk sec/Read, Available MBytes
journalctl       Event Viewer ; Get-WinEvent
df / du          Get-Volume ; TreeSize / WinDirStat

# which process owns port 443?
Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 443 | Select OwningProcess
Get-Process -Id <pid>

# disk cleanup on a full C:
Dism /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup
concepts.tip: perfmon counter 'Avg. Disk sec/Read' over 20 ms = storage is the bottleneck, same idea as iostat await.

concepts.what: Windows' web server. Sites bind to IP, port and host header; each app runs in an application pool (a w3wp.exe worker process with its own identity).
concepts.why: If the shop runs .NET, onboarding a Windows app means IIS.
concepts.ex:
Get-Website
Get-IISAppPool
Restart-WebAppPool -Name MyAppPool
# logs
C:\inetpub\logs\LogFiles\W3SVC1\
# common errors
503  app pool stopped (often crashed or the service account password expired)
500.19  bad web.config
401  auth config (Windows auth vs anonymous)
concepts.tip: App pool keeps stopping = rapid-fail protection after repeated crashes. Check the Application event log for the real error.

qa.q: What is a domain controller?
qa.a: A server running Active Directory Domain Services. It authenticates users and computers, holds the directory, applies policy, and replicates with other DCs. You run at least two for redundancy.

qa.q: OU vs security group?
qa.a: An OU is a container for organizing objects and linking GPOs. A security group is for granting permissions. GPOs link to OUs, not groups.

qa.q: A GPO isn't applying. How do you troubleshoot?
qa.a: Run `gpresult /r` to see what applied. Check the GPO is linked to the right OU and the object is actually in that OU. Check security filtering. Run `gpupdate /force`. Check DNS, because clients find DCs through DNS.

qa.q: A user has Full Control on the share but can't write. Why?
qa.a: NTFS permissions are more restrictive. Effective access is the most restrictive of share and NTFS. Check the Effective Access tab on the folder.

qa.q: Kerberos vs NTLM?
qa.a: Kerberos is ticket-based, the default for domain logins, and needs working DNS and clocks within 5 minutes. NTLM is the older challenge/response fallback, used when Kerberos can't work, like connecting by IP address.

qa.q: A server's clock is 10 minutes off. What breaks?
qa.a: Kerberos fails after 5 minutes of skew, so logins and service authentication break. Fix with `w32tm /resync`, and make sure the PDC Emulator syncs to a reliable external time source.

qa.q: A server rebooted overnight. How do you find out why?
qa.a: Check the System log: 1074 shows a planned restart and who or what requested it (often Windows Update or SCCM). 6008 or 41 means an unexpected shutdown or crash, so look for a crash dump next.

qa.q: A service won't start with error 1053. What do you check?
qa.a: It didn't respond in time. Check its dependencies (`sc qc name`), the service account and password, and the Application log for the real error underneath.

qa.q: RDP isn't working. Checklist?
qa.a: Remote Desktop enabled, TermService running, firewall allows 3389, user is in Remote Desktop Users, NLA settings match, and on an RD host the licensing grace period hasn't run out.

qa.q: How do you roll back a bad Windows patch across many servers?
qa.a: Stop the rollout in WSUS or SCCM first. Uninstall with `wusa /uninstall /kb:<id>` pushed through SCCM or a script, or revert snapshots for critical servers. Decline the update so it doesn't reinstall, confirm services are healthy, and document it in the change record.

qa.q: How do you find which process owns a port on Windows?
qa.a: `netstat -ano | findstr :443` gives the PID; `tasklist /fi "pid eq <pid>"` or `Get-Process -Id <pid>` names it. PowerShell: `Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort 443 | Select OwningProcess`.

qa.q: A Windows server is slow. What do you check?
qa.a: Task Manager and Resource Monitor for the top CPU, memory, disk and network consumer. perfmon counters: % Processor Time, Available MBytes, Avg. Disk sec/Read and Write (over 20 ms is bad), Disk Queue Length. Event logs for errors. Then the hypervisor side: CPU ready, ballooning, datastore latency.

qa.q: An IIS site returns 503. What do you check?
qa.a: The app pool is probably stopped. Check its state with `Get-IISAppPool`. If it keeps stopping, rapid-fail protection is tripping on repeated crashes: read the Application event log. A classic cause is the app pool service account's password expiring or the account getting locked.

qa.q: C: drive is full on a Windows server. What do you do?
qa.a: Find the space with TreeSize/WinDirStat or PowerShell. Usual suspects: IIS logs, temp folders, old user profiles, crash dumps, WinSxS. Clean component store with `Dism /Online /Cleanup-Image /StartComponentCleanup`, move logs off C:, set log retention, and grow the disk if it's simply undersized.

topics.name: Networking
topics.blurb: OSI layers, subnets, DNS, TCP/UDP, firewalls

concepts.what: L2 = MAC addresses and switches. L3 = IP addresses and routers. L4 = TCP/UDP ports. L7 = HTTP and the application.
concepts.why: 'L4 vs L7 load balancer' and 'which layer is the problem' both need this.
concepts.ex:
L2  Data link   MAC, switches, VLANs      ip link, arp -n
L3  Network     IP, routing               ip r, ping, traceroute
L4  Transport   TCP/UDP ports             ss -tlnp, nc -zv
L7  Application HTTP, DNS, TLS            curl -v, dig
concepts.tip: Start at the bottom and stop at the first layer that fails.

concepts.what: The /number is how many bits are the network. Fewer network bits = more hosts.
concepts.why: You'll get at least one subnet question.
concepts.tip: Each step up (/24 → /25) halves the addresses.

concepts.what: Your resolver asks root → TLD (.com) → the authoritative server for the domain. Answers are cached for the record's TTL.
concepts.why: 'It's always DNS' is a joke because it's usually true.
concepts.ex:
dig app.example.com
dig +trace app.example.com     # full lookup path
dig @8.8.8.8 app.example.com   # ask a specific resolver
dig -x 10.0.0.5                # reverse lookup

A     name → IPv4        CNAME  alias → another name
PTR   IP → name          MX     mail server
SRV   service location   TXT    verification, SPF
concepts.tip: Lower the TTL a day before a planned IP change.

concepts.t: What happens when you open a URL
concepts.what: DNS lookup → TCP handshake → TLS handshake → HTTP request → load balancer → web/app server → response → browser renders.
concepts.why: Asked in nearly every infra interview. Say it in 30 seconds.
concepts.ex:
curl -v https://app.example.com
# * Trying 203.0.113.10:443        (DNS done, TCP connecting)
# * SSL connection using TLSv1.3   (TLS handshake)
# > GET / HTTP/2                   (request)
# < HTTP/2 200                     (response)
concepts.tip: Mention the load balancer. That's your world.

concepts.what: Stateful firewalls track connections, so return traffic is allowed automatically. Stateless ACLs need rules both ways.
concepts.why: You file firewall requests constantly; know what goes in one.
concepts.ex:
Firewall request needs:
  source IP/subnet
  destination IP
  port + protocol (TCP 443)
  direction
  business reason

Verify after:  nc -zv dest 443   |   Test-NetConnection dest -Port 443
concepts.tip: If the backend calls back to the client, you need a rule in that direction too.

concepts.what: Open: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Close: FIN/ACK from each side; the side that closes first sits in TIME_WAIT for a while. RST = abrupt reset (nothing listening, or a firewall rejecting).
concepts.why: Reading a packet capture or `ss` output depends on this, and 'explain the 3-way handshake' is a standard question.
concepts.ex:
Client                     Server
  SYN  ------------------->          (connect starts)
       <-------------- SYN-ACK      (port open, listening)
  ACK  ------------------->          (established)

SYN, no answer         = dropped (firewall/NSG/routing) -> 'timed out'
SYN, RST back          = nothing listening / rejected   -> 'connection refused'

ss -tan | awk '{print $1}' | sort | uniq -c   # count states
LISTEN  ESTAB  TIME-WAIT  CLOSE-WAIT  SYN-SENT
concepts.tip: Lots of CLOSE_WAIT = the app isn't closing its sockets (app bug). Lots of SYN_SENT = it can't reach the destination.

concepts.what: Client Hello (versions, ciphers, SNI hostname) → Server Hello + certificate chain → key exchange → encrypted traffic. TLS 1.3 does it in one round trip.
concepts.why: Explains cert errors, SNI problems and why TLS adds latency.
concepts.ex:
openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 -servername app.example.com -brief
curl -v https://app.example.com 2>&1 | grep -E 'SSL|TLS|subject|issuer|expire'

Common failures
  unknown CA / unable to get local issuer  -> missing intermediate or private CA not trusted
  hostname mismatch                         -> name not in SAN
  handshake failure                         -> no shared TLS version/cipher
  wrong cert served                         -> SNI missing (-servername)
concepts.tip: SNI lets one IP serve many certificates. Testing by IP without `-servername` gets you the default cert and a misleading error.

concepts.what: Methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), headers (Host, Authorization, X-Forwarded-For, Cache-Control), status classes (2xx ok, 3xx redirect, 4xx client, 5xx server), keep-alive connection reuse.
concepts.why: Most of what an LB, WAF or reverse proxy does is about HTTP.
concepts.ex:
curl -I https://app.example.com              # headers only
curl -H 'Host: app.example.com' http://10.2.0.11:8080/   # hit one backend directly
curl -L -v http://app.example.com             # follow redirects, see each hop

301/302  redirect (http->https, login)
401      not authenticated     403  authenticated but not allowed
404      wrong path/route      429  rate limited
500      app bug               502/503/504  proxy/backend problem
concepts.tip: Hitting a backend directly with the right Host header tells you whether the problem is the app or the LB in front of it.

concepts.what: Forward proxy: clients go out through it (corporate web proxy). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers (Nginx, F5). DHCP: Discover, Offer, Request, Ack. ARP: maps an IP to a MAC on the local subnet.
concepts.why: 'Works from my laptop, fails from the server' is often the proxy. 'Duplicate IP' is ARP.
concepts.ex:
env | grep -i proxy                      # HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY, NO_PROXY
curl -x http://proxy.corp:8080 https://api.vendor.com
export NO_PROXY=localhost,127.0.0.1,.corp.local,10.0.0.0/8

ip neigh ; arping -D -I eth0 10.2.0.50   # duplicate IP check
DHCP: Discover -> Offer -> Request -> Ack (DORA)
concepts.tip: Internal calls going to the proxy and failing = NO_PROXY missing the internal domain.

qa.q: TCP vs UDP?
qa.a: TCP is connection-based, ordered and retransmits lost packets: HTTP, SSH, databases. UDP is fire-and-forget with less overhead: DNS, NTP, video and voice.

qa.q: What happens when you type a URL into a browser?
qa.a: The browser resolves the name through DNS, opens a TCP connection, does a TLS handshake for HTTPS, and sends the HTTP request. It usually hits a load balancer, which forwards to a backend server. The response comes back and the browser renders it.

qa.q: What is a default gateway?
qa.a: The router a machine sends traffic to when the destination isn't on its own subnet. A wrong gateway means you can reach local machines but nothing beyond.

qa.q: Name common ports.
qa.a: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3389 RDP, 389/636 LDAP/LDAPS, 445 SMB, 1433 SQL Server, 3306 MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 6443 Kubernetes API.

qa.q: How many usable hosts in a /26?
qa.a: 64 addresses, 62 usable (minus network and broadcast).

qa.q: What is a VLAN?
qa.a: A logical network segment on a switch. Devices in different VLANs need a router or Layer 3 switch to talk. Trunk ports carry several VLANs using 802.1Q tags.

qa.q: What is NAT?
qa.a: Network Address Translation rewrites addresses at the edge. Source NAT lets private hosts reach the internet through one public IP. Destination NAT (port forwarding) sends inbound traffic to an internal server.

qa.q: Ping works but the app port times out. What does that tell you?
qa.a: The network path is fine. Something is blocking or not listening on that port: a firewall or security group, or the app isn't running or is bound to localhost. Check with `nc -zv` from the client and `ss -tlnp` on the server.

qa.q: What is MTU and why does it matter?
qa.a: The largest packet size, usually 1500 bytes. A mismatch, common over VPNs and tunnels, makes small requests work while large transfers hang. Test with `ping -M do -s 1472 host`.

qa.q: What is split-horizon DNS?
qa.a: The same name resolves to different answers inside and outside the network: an internal IP for employees, a public VIP for everyone else.

qa.q: You changed a DNS record and half the users still reach the old IP. Why, and how do you avoid it?
qa.a: Resolvers and clients cached the old answer until its TTL runs out. Next time, lower the TTL to about 5 minutes a day before the change, make the change, confirm, then raise it again.

qa.q: Explain the TCP three-way handshake.
qa.a: Client sends SYN, server answers SYN-ACK, client sends ACK; the connection is established. If the SYN gets no answer, something dropped it (timeout). If it gets a RST, the host was reached but nothing is listening or it was rejected (refused).

qa.q: What does ARP do?
qa.a: Finds the MAC address for an IP on the local subnet so the frame can be delivered. For remote destinations the host ARPs for its default gateway. `ip neigh` or `arp -a` shows the cache.

qa.q: Forward proxy vs reverse proxy?
qa.a: A forward proxy acts for clients going out (corporate web proxy, filtering, caching). A reverse proxy acts for servers, receiving incoming traffic and passing it to backends (Nginx, F5, App Gateway).

qa.q: An app works by IP but not by hostname. What's wrong?
qa.a: Name resolution or name-based config. Check DNS (`getent hosts`, `dig`), the hosts file, and search domains. If it resolves fine, the server may route by Host header or SNI, so the IP gets a default site or the wrong certificate.

qa.q: Lots of connections stuck in CLOSE_WAIT. What does it mean?
qa.a: The remote side closed, but the local application never closed its socket. It's an application bug (connection leak), not a network problem. It eventually exhausts file descriptors or connection pools; restart buys time, the fix is in the code.

qa.q: A server can't reach an external API but your laptop can. Likely causes?
qa.a: The server needs a proxy (check HTTP_PROXY/HTTPS_PROXY), the firewall or NSG blocks egress from that subnet, the server can't resolve the external name, or the API allowlists source IPs and the server's NAT IP isn't on the list. Test with `curl -v` with and without `-x proxy`.

qa.q: What is SNI and why does it matter?
qa.a: Server Name Indication: the client sends the hostname in the TLS Client Hello so one IP can serve many certificates. Old clients or tests by IP without SNI get the default certificate and a name-mismatch error.

qa.q: Explain asymmetric routing and why firewalls hate it.
qa.a: Request goes out one path and the reply comes back another. A stateful firewall that only sees one direction drops the traffic because it never saw the SYN. Common in Azure with UDRs sending traffic to a firewall one way only, or dual WAN links on-prem. Fix by making routing symmetric or using SNAT at the firewall.

qa.q: How would you implement a logical network overlay between distributed nodes to ensure isolation and reliable communication, and which protocols or technologies would you use?
qa.a: I would use technologies like VXLAN or WireGuard to create an overlay network, providing isolation and encrypted communication between nodes. VXLAN encapsulates Layer 2 frames within UDP packets, allowing for scalable virtual networks, while WireGuard offers a simpler, secure VPN tunnel. Both approaches enable logical segmentation regardless of the underlying physical network.

qa.q: How would you troubleshoot intermittent packet loss in a microservices architecture running on Kubernetes, considering recent changes in CNI (Container Network Interface) plugins and overlay networking?
qa.a: I would first check the CNI plugin logs for errors or dropped packets, then use tools like `kubectl exec` with `tcpdump` to trace packets between pods. I'd verify MTU settings and overlay network configurations, since mismatches can cause fragmentation or drops. Reviewing recent CNI plugin updates for known issues and ensuring all nodes use compatible configurations is also essential.

qa.q: How would you use the Linux `AF_PACKET` socket family with `PACKET_FANOUT` to efficiently distribute incoming packets across multiple threads, and what are some common pitfalls that can disrupt even load balancing?
qa.a: To efficiently distribute packets, you can use `AF_PACKET` sockets with the `PACKET_FANOUT_LB` option, which load-balances packets in a round-robin fashion among threads. A common pitfall is that if one thread's socket buffer fills up or a thread is slower, the kernel may skip it, breaking strict round-robin. Monitoring buffer usage and tuning thread processing rates are crucial for consistent distribution.

qa.q: What are the advantages and potential drawbacks of using DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) compared to traditional DNS, especially in enterprise network environments?
qa.a: DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) encrypts DNS queries, improving privacy and preventing interception or manipulation by intermediaries. However, it can bypass enterprise DNS filtering and monitoring, complicating security enforcement and troubleshooting. Administrators may need to configure firewalls or endpoint policies to manage DoH traffic appropriately.

qa.q: How would you design a scalable, low-latency UDP-based communication layer for a real-time multiplayer game, and what networking challenges would you need to address to ensure reliability and fairness among players?
qa.a: I would use UDP for minimal latency and implement custom reliability mechanisms, such as sequence numbers and acknowledgments, to handle packet loss and out-of-order delivery. To ensure fairness, I'd monitor network jitter and latency, possibly using techniques like lag compensation and server-side reconciliation. I'd also use NAT traversal (e.g., STUN) to connect players behind firewalls and closely monitor DDoS risks and rate limiting to prevent abuse.

qa.q: What are some considerations and best practices when configuring firewall rules to support DNS-over-HTTPS (DoH) while maintaining network observability and security?
qa.a: When enabling DoH, you should allow outbound HTTPS traffic on port 443 to trusted DoH resolvers, but also monitor for unauthorized DoH endpoints to prevent data exfiltration. Use deep packet inspection or allow-listed resolver IPs to maintain visibility, and update firewall logging to capture DoH traffic patterns for security auditing.

concepts.what: VIP = the address clients hit. Pool = the backend servers. Monitor = the health check. Persistence = same client to same server. Algorithm = round robin, least connections, weighted.
concepts.why: Load balancers come up in almost every infra interview. Use the exact words.
concepts.ex:
Client → DNS app.example.com → VIP 10.1.1.50:443
          │
          ▼  TLS terminated, health checks on /health
     ┌─────────────┐
     │ Pool: app   │  round robin
     │ 10.2.0.11:8080 ✔
     │ 10.2.0.12:8080 ✔
     │ 10.2.0.13:8080 ✘ (failed check, removed)
     └─────────────┘
concepts.tip: Onboarding story shape: gather VIP, pool, ports, health check URL, cert and persistence needs, submit to the LB team, validate backends, test end to end.

concepts.what: L4 balances on IP and port without reading the traffic. L7 reads HTTP, so it can route by host or path, rewrite headers, terminate TLS and run a WAF.
concepts.why: Asked in almost every infra interview.
concepts.ex:
L4 (TCP):  10.1.1.50:5432 → db pool        fast, any protocol
L7 (HTTP): app.example.com/api → api pool
           app.example.com/    → web pool
concepts.tip: Products: F5, Nginx, HAProxy, AWS ALB (L7) and NLB (L4), Azure App Gateway (L7) and Load Balancer (L4).

concepts.what: Nginx accepts client traffic and forwards it to backend servers (an upstream).
concepts.why: Nginx shows up almost everywhere.
concepts.tip: Always `nginx -t` before reload. Reload is zero-downtime; restart isn't.

concepts.what: A cert holds a public key and an identity, signed by a CA. The chain goes leaf → intermediate → root. The private key never leaves the server.
concepts.why: Expired or broken certs cause real outages.
concepts.ex:
# key + CSR
openssl req -new -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes \
  -keyout app.key -out app.csr -subj "/CN=app.example.com"

# check a live site's chain and expiry
openssl s_client -connect app.example.com:443 -servername app.example.com

# read a cert file
openssl x509 -in app.crt -noout -subject -dates -ext subjectAltName
concepts.tip: Formats: PEM = text (.crt/.key), PFX = key + cert bundle with a password (Windows).

concepts.what: 502, 503 and 504 each point to a different problem behind the proxy.
concepts.why: You'll be asked to read these.
concepts.ex:
502 Bad Gateway         backend refused or sent garbage
503 Service Unavailable no healthy members in the pool
504 Gateway Timeout     backend too slow to answer

401/403  auth problem      404  wrong path or route
concepts.tip: 503 after a deploy? Check whether the health check path still exists.

concepts.t: F5 BIG-IP objects (what the LB team actually builds)
concepts.what: Node (server IP) → Pool (nodes + port + monitor + LB method) → Virtual Server (VIP:port) with profiles (TCP, HTTP, client-SSL, server-SSL), SNAT (often Automap) and persistence. iRules/LTM policies add logic.
concepts.why: If you 'submitted VIP requests', a panel will ask what got configured. Knowing the objects separates an engineer from a ticket router.
concepts.ex:
tmsh list ltm virtual vs_app_443
tmsh show ltm pool pool_app_8080 members      # member up/down + why
tmsh list ltm monitor http mon_app_health

# HTTP monitor send/receive string
send: GET /health HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: app.example.com\r\nConnection: close\r\n\r\n
recv: 200 OK

# packet capture on F5 with LB context
tcpdump -ni 0.0:nnn host 10.2.0.11 and port 8080

SNAT Automap: backend sees the F5 self-IP as the source
  -> return traffic comes back through the F5 (symmetric)
  -> client IP lost unless X-Forwarded-For is inserted
concepts.tip: Why SNAT? Without it the server replies directly to the client, bypassing the F5, and the connection breaks (asymmetric).

concepts.what: Four services, two questions: global or regional? HTTP(S) or any TCP/UDP?
concepts.why: 'Which Azure LB would you use?' is near-certain in an Azure interview.
concepts.ex:
Scope      Layer   Use it for
Load Balancer    regional   L4      any TCP/UDP, VMs/VMSS, internal or public
App Gateway      regional   L7      HTTP(S), path/host routing, WAF, TLS offload
Front Door       global     L7      internet apps, global anycast, CDN, WAF
Traffic Manager  global     DNS     DNS-based failover/geo, any protocol

Common combos
  Front Door -> App Gateway (WAF) -> VMs/AKS    (global external app)
  internal LB -> VMs                           (internal TCP service)
  App Gateway (private IP) -> VMs               (internal web app)
concepts.tip: Azure LB health probes come from `168.63.129.16`. A custom NSG deny-all above the default AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound rule marks every backend down.

concepts.what: A `/health` (liveness: process is up) and `/ready` (dependencies reachable) endpoint that returns 200 fast, without auth, and doesn't do heavy work.
concepts.why: Bad health checks cause more 'mysterious' outages than LBs themselves.
concepts.ex:
Good
  GET /health -> 200 in < 100 ms, no login, no redirect
  interval 5-10 s, ~3 failures to mark down, ~2 passes to mark up

Bad
  /  that redirects to SSO (302)       -> always 'down'
  check that queries the DB heavily     -> DB slow = every node pulled = full outage
  TCP-only check                        -> app hung but port open = still 'up'
concepts.tip: If the check depends on a shared dependency, one DB blip removes ALL members. Decide deliberately what 'healthy' means.

qa.q: L4 vs L7 load balancer?
qa.a: L4 balances on IP and port and doesn't look inside; it's fast and works for any TCP/UDP. L7 understands HTTP, so it can route by host or path, terminate TLS, rewrite headers and run a WAF.

qa.q: What is a health check and what happens when it fails?
qa.a: The LB probes each backend on a schedule, like a TCP connect or an HTTP GET expecting 200. A member that fails is pulled out of rotation until it passes again.
502: the proxy reached the backend but got a bad or refused response. 503: no healthy backends. 504: the backend took too long to answer.

qa.q: When do you use sticky sessions, and what's the downside?
qa.a: When the app keeps session data in local memory. Downsides: uneven load, and users lose their session if that server dies. Better fix: store sessions in Redis or a database so any server can handle any request.

qa.q: The backend logs show the LB's IP instead of the client's. Fix?
qa.a: Turn on the X-Forwarded-For header on the L7 load balancer and configure the web server to log it. For L4, use proxy protocol or route return traffic through the LB without SNAT.

qa.q: A VIP returns 503 right after a deploy. Where do you look?
qa.a: Pool member health. Often the app team changed or removed the health check path, so every member fails the monitor even though the app runs. Fix the monitor or restore the path.

qa.q: The browser says 'not secure' but the cert is valid. Why?
qa.a: Usually the intermediate certificate isn't installed, so the chain is incomplete. `openssl s_client` shows it. Add the intermediate to the chain on the LB or web server.

qa.q: What is a SAN on a certificate? What about wildcards?
qa.a: Subject Alternative Names let one cert cover several hostnames. A wildcard like `*.example.com` covers one level of subdomains, not the bare domain or deeper levels.

qa.q: Active-active vs active-passive load balancers?
qa.a: Active-passive: one unit serves, the other waits and takes over the floating IP on failure. Active-active: both serve traffic for more capacity, but session state must be synced.

qa.q: A cert expired at 2 a.m. and the site is down. Fix it and prevent it.
qa.a: Now: issue or renew the cert, install it with the intermediate on the LB, reload, verify with `openssl s_client`. Prevent: keep an inventory of every cert and its expiry, alert at 30, 14 and 7 days, and automate renewal (ACME or Key Vault) where possible.

qa.q: Where should TLS terminate?
qa.a: Usually at the load balancer: one place to manage certs, the WAF can see the traffic, backends do less work. If compliance needs encryption end to end, re-encrypt from the LB to the backends.

qa.q: What does SNAT do on a load balancer?
qa.a: Rewrites the client's source IP to the LB's own IP before sending to the backend, so the backend's reply comes back through the LB. Downside: the backend no longer sees the real client IP, so you insert X-Forwarded-For.

qa.q: Pool members show down but the app works when you curl it. Why?
qa.a: The monitor doesn't match reality: wrong path, Host header missing (send string), expects '200 OK' but gets a 302 to login, HTTPS monitor against an HTTP port, or the LB's self-IP/probe source is blocked by the host firewall or NSG. Test from the LB itself, with the exact monitor request.

qa.q: Azure Load Balancer vs Application Gateway vs Front Door vs Traffic Manager?
qa.a: Load Balancer: regional L4, any TCP/UDP. App Gateway: regional L7 with WAF, TLS offload and path routing. Front Door: global L7 edge with anycast, CDN and WAF for internet apps. Traffic Manager: DNS-based global routing and failover for any protocol. Pick by global vs regional and HTTP vs not.

qa.q: How do you test a new VIP before DNS points at it?
qa.a: `curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:<VIP> https://app.example.com/health` (or a hosts-file entry). It sends the right SNI and Host header to the new VIP, so you validate cert, routing and backends before go-live. Then go-live is just the DNS change.

qa.q: A health check that queries the database caused a full outage. Explain and fix.
qa.a: The DB slowed down, every member failed its check at once, and the LB removed all of them: a small degradation became a total outage. Make liveness checks cheap and local, use readiness for dependencies carefully, and alert on dependency health separately instead of pulling every node.

concepts.what: An image is a read-only template built in layers. A container is a running instance of an image with its own thin writable layer on top.
concepts.why: Every container interview starts here.
concepts.ex:
docker pull nginx:1.27
docker images
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:1.27
docker ps            # running
docker ps -a         # include stopped
docker stop web && docker rm web
concepts.tip: Image = the class. Container = the object.

concepts.what: A VM virtualizes hardware and runs its own kernel. A container shares the host kernel and isolates processes with namespaces (what it can see) and cgroups (how much it can use).
concepts.why: Connects containers to virtualization concepts you may already know.
concepts.ex:
VM:         App │ Libs │ Guest OS │ Hypervisor │ Hardware
            minutes to boot, GBs, strong isolation

Container:  App │ Libs │ Container runtime │ Host OS │ Hardware
            seconds to start, MBs, shares the host kernel
concepts.tip: VMs for isolation and legacy apps; containers for packaging and scaling apps.

concepts.what: A recipe for building an image. Each instruction adds a layer.
concepts.why: You'll be asked to read or write one.
concepts.ex:
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY . .
USER 1000
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["gunicorn", "-b", "0.0.0.0:8000", "app:app"]

docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
concepts.tip: Copy the dependency file before the code, so the slow install layer stays cached when only code changes.

concepts.what: Build in one stage with all the tools, then copy only the result into a small runtime image.
concepts.why: Smaller images, fewer vulnerabilities. A common follow-up question.
concepts.ex:
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN mvn -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build /src/target/app.jar /app.jar
USER 1000
CMD ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]
concepts.tip: The final image has no Maven, no source code, just the JAR and a JRE.

concepts.what: Containers lose their writable layer when removed. Volumes (managed by Docker) and bind mounts (a host folder) keep data outside the container.
concepts.why: 'Our data disappeared' is a classic question.
concepts.ex:
docker volume create pgdata
docker run -d --name db \
  -v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data postgres:16

# bind mount a host folder, read-only
docker run -d -v /srv/config:/etc/app:ro myapp:1.0

docker volume ls
docker volume inspect pgdata
concepts.tip: Databases always get a volume.

concepts.what: Default bridge network gives each container a private IP. User-defined networks add DNS so containers find each other by name. `-p host:container` publishes a port.
concepts.why: 'Containers can't talk to each other' comes up a lot.
concepts.ex:
docker network create appnet
docker run -d --network appnet --name db postgres:16
docker run -d --network appnet -p 8080:8000 --name api myapp:1.0
# api reaches the database at host name 'db'

docker network inspect appnet
concepts.tip: `-p 8080:80` = host port 8080 goes to container port 80.

concepts.what: Define a multi-container app in one YAML file and start it with one command.
concepts.why: Standard for local and small single-host setups.
concepts.ex:
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8000"]
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
    depends_on: [db]
  db:
    image: postgres:16
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: example
    volumes: [pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
volumes:
  pgdata:

docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f api
docker compose down
concepts.tip: Compose runs on one host. Across many hosts you need Kubernetes.

concepts.what: The commands you reach for when a container misbehaves.
concepts.why: Interviewers ask 'the container keeps exiting, what do you do?'
concepts.ex:
docker logs --tail 100 -f web     # what did it print?
docker ps -a                      # exit code in STATUS
docker inspect web --format '{{.State.ExitCode}} {{.State.OOMKilled}}'
docker exec -it web sh            # get a shell inside
docker stats                      # live CPU/memory
docker system df                  # disk used by images/volumes
docker system prune               # clean up unused stuff
concepts.tip: Exit 137 = killed (often out of memory). Exit 1 = app error. Exit 0 = main process just finished.

concepts.what: Images are stored in registries: Docker Hub, Azure Container Registry, AWS ECR, Artifactory. A tag names a version.
concepts.why: Every pipeline pushes to a registry.
concepts.ex:
docker tag myapp:1.0 myacr.azurecr.io/myapp:1.0
docker login myacr.azurecr.io
docker push myacr.azurecr.io/myapp:1.0
docker pull myacr.azurecr.io/myapp:1.0
concepts.tip: Don't deploy `:latest` to prod; pin a version so you know what's running.

qa.q: Container vs virtual machine?
qa.a: A VM has its own kernel on a hypervisor, takes minutes to boot and is heavier. A container shares the host kernel, isolates processes with namespaces and cgroups, starts in seconds and is much smaller. VMs give stronger isolation; containers are better for packaging and scaling apps.

qa.q: Image vs container?
qa.a: An image is the read-only template. A container is a running instance of it with a writable layer. One image can run many containers.

qa.q: What does -p 8080:80 mean?
qa.a: Publish the container's port 80 on the host's port 8080. Traffic to host:8080 goes to the container's port 80.

qa.q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?
qa.a: ENTRYPOINT sets the fixed executable. CMD gives default arguments that `docker run` can override. Together: ENTRYPOINT is the program, CMD is its default flags.

qa.q: COPY vs ADD?
qa.a: COPY copies files from the build context. ADD also unpacks local tar files and can fetch URLs. Prefer COPY because it's predictable.

qa.q: A container exits right after it starts. How do you troubleshoot?
qa.a: `docker ps -a` for the exit code, `docker logs` for the output. Common causes: the main process finished (it must run in the foreground), a bad command or config, a missing env var. Exit 137 means it was killed, often out of memory.

qa.q: Data disappeared when the container was recreated. Why, and how do you fix it?
qa.a: Data written inside the container lives in its writable layer, which is deleted with the container. Store it in a named volume or a bind mount instead.

qa.q: How do you make an image smaller?
qa.a: Use a slim or distroless base, use multi-stage builds, combine RUN steps and clean package caches in the same step, and add a `.dockerignore` so you don't copy junk into the build.

qa.q: Two containers can't reach each other by name. Why?
qa.a: They're on the default bridge network, which has no name resolution. Put them on a user-defined network (`docker network create`) and they can find each other by container name.

qa.q: What restart policies exist?
qa.a: `no` (default), `on-failure` (restart on non-zero exit), `always`, and `unless-stopped` (always, unless you stopped it by hand).

qa.q: What does exit code 137 mean?
qa.a: The process got SIGKILL, most often from the out-of-memory killer. Confirm with `docker inspect` (State.OOMKilled) and raise the memory limit or fix the app.

qa.q: Docker Compose vs Kubernetes?
qa.a: Compose runs a multi-container app on one host, good for dev and small setups. Kubernetes runs containers across many nodes with scheduling, self-healing, scaling and rolling updates.

qa.q: How do you secure containers?
qa.a: Run as a non-root user, use minimal base images, scan images for CVEs (Trivy, Defender), never bake secrets into images (inject at runtime), pin image versions, set CPU and memory limits, and use a read-only filesystem where possible.

qa.q: How does a container stay isolated if it shares the kernel?
qa.a: Namespaces control what it can see: its own process list, network, mounts and hostname. cgroups control how much CPU and memory it can use. Extra layers like seccomp, AppArmor or SELinux limit which system calls it can make.

qa.q: How can you configure a Docker Compose service to automatically run a database initialization script when the container starts, ensuring the script executes only once even if the container restarts?
qa.a: You can use the `entrypoint` or `command` directive in your Docker Compose file to call a shell script that checks for a marker file (e.g., `/data/.initialized`). If the file doesn't exist, the script runs the initialization commands and creates the marker file. This prevents re-running the script on container restart, and works well with persistent volumes.

qa.q: How can you use Docker's BuildKit to optimize multi-stage builds for faster image creation, and what BuildKit-specific features would you enable in your Dockerfile?
qa.a: Using BuildKit, you can leverage cache mounts and secrets management in your Dockerfile to optimize multi-stage builds. For example, you can use the `--mount=type=cache` option in RUN steps to cache dependencies, and `--mount=type=secret` for securely passing credentials during build. Enabling BuildKit (`DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1`) allows these features, resulting in faster and more secure builds.

concepts.what: The control plane makes decisions; worker nodes run the containers.
concepts.why: First question in almost every Kubernetes round.
concepts.ex:
CONTROL PLANE
  kube-apiserver        front door, every command goes through it
  etcd                  key-value store holding all cluster state
  kube-scheduler        picks a node for each new pod
  controller-manager    keeps actual state = desired state

WORKER NODE
  kubelet               runs pods on this node, reports health
  kube-proxy            routes Service traffic to pods
  containerd            container runtime

kubectl get nodes -o wide
kubectl get pods -n kube-system
concepts.tip: You declare what you want; controllers keep making it true.

concepts.what: The smallest unit. One or more containers that share an IP and storage and always run on the same node. Pods are disposable.
concepts.why: Everything else in Kubernetes manages pods.
concepts.ex:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: web
  labels: { app: web }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: web
    image: nginx:1.27
    ports:
    - containerPort: 80

kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pods -o wide
concepts.tip: You rarely create bare pods. Deployments create them for you.

concepts.what: Keeps a set number of identical pods running through a ReplicaSet, and handles rolling updates and rollbacks.
concepts.why: The workload you'll talk about most.
concepts.ex:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: web }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: web }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web
        image: myacr.azurecr.io/web:1.4

kubectl scale deploy web --replicas=5
