kubectl set image deploy/web web=myacr.azurecr.io/web:1.5
kubectl rollout status deploy/web
kubectl rollout undo deploy/web
concepts.tip: Deployment → ReplicaSet → Pods. Delete a pod and the ReplicaSet makes a new one.

concepts.what: A stable IP and DNS name in front of a changing set of pods, chosen by labels.
concepts.why: Pods die and get new IPs; Services give clients something stable.
concepts.ex:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: web }
spec:
  type: ClusterIP          # or NodePort, LoadBalancer
  selector: { app: web }
  ports:
  - port: 80
    targetPort: 8080

ClusterIP     internal only (default)
NodePort      opens a port on every node (30000–32767)
LoadBalancer  asks the cloud for an external load balancer

kubectl get svc
kubectl get endpoints web    # empty = no matching ready pods
concepts.tip: Inside the cluster, call it at web.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local.

concepts.what: L7 HTTP routing into the cluster by host and path, with TLS. Needs an ingress controller (Nginx, Traefik, App Gateway) to actually work.
concepts.why: It's a load balancer, which is your home turf.
concepts.ex:
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata: { name: app }
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts: [app.example.com]
    secretName: app-tls
  rules:
  - host: app.example.com
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /api
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: { service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } } }
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend: { service: { name: web, port: { number: 80 } } }
concepts.tip: Internet → cloud LB → ingress controller → Service → pods.

concepts.what: Keep config out of the image. ConfigMaps hold plain settings; Secrets hold passwords and keys. Both mount as files or env vars.
concepts.why: Asked as 'how do you handle config and passwords?'
concepts.ex:
kubectl create configmap app-cfg --from-literal=LOG_LEVEL=info
kubectl create secret generic db-pass --from-literal=password=S3cret

# in the container spec
envFrom:
- configMapRef: { name: app-cfg }
env:
- name: DB_PASSWORD
  valueFrom:
    secretKeyRef: { name: db-pass, key: password }
concepts.tip: Secrets are only base64-encoded unless encryption at rest or an external vault is set up.

concepts.what: Liveness: restart the container if it hangs. Readiness: stop sending traffic until it's ready. Startup: give slow apps time before liveness starts.
concepts.why: Wrong probes cause restart loops and outages.
concepts.ex:
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /healthz, port: 8080 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 10
  periodSeconds: 10
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /ready, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
concepts.tip: Readiness is the Kubernetes version of an LB health check.

concepts.what: Requests are what the scheduler reserves for a container. Limits are the ceiling. Over the CPU limit = throttled. Over the memory limit = killed (OOMKilled).
concepts.why: Explains Pending pods, slow pods and OOMKilled pods.
concepts.ex:
resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 250m        # a quarter of a core
    memory: 256Mi
  limits:
    cpu: "1"
    memory: 512Mi

kubectl top pods
kubectl describe node <node>   # allocated vs capacity
concepts.tip: No requests set = the scheduler is guessing.

concepts.what: PersistentVolume (PV) = a piece of storage. PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) = a pod's request for storage. StorageClass = creates PVs automatically.
concepts.why: Storage is an infra topic even in Kubernetes.
concepts.ex:
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: data }
spec:
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
  storageClassName: managed-csi
  resources:
    requests: { storage: 20Gi }

kubectl get pvc,pv
concepts.tip: A PVC stuck Pending usually means no matching StorageClass or capacity.

concepts.what: Different controllers for different jobs.
concepts.why: 'Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet' is a standard question.
concepts.ex:
Deployment   stateless apps, interchangeable pods
StatefulSet  stable names (db-0, db-1) + own storage each: databases
DaemonSet    one pod on every node: log and monitoring agents
Job          run to completion once: migrations
CronJob      Job on a schedule: nightly reports

kubectl autoscale deploy web --min=2 --max=10 --cpu-percent=70
kubectl get hpa
concepts.tip: Your monitoring agent (Dynatrace, node-exporter) runs as a DaemonSet.

concepts.what: The order to check things when a pod misbehaves.
concepts.why: The practical half of every Kubernetes interview.
concepts.ex:
kubectl get pods -A | grep -v Running
kubectl describe pod <pod>          # read Events at the bottom
kubectl logs <pod> --previous       # output from the crashed run
kubectl logs <pod> -c <container>
kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp
kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh
kubectl get endpoints <svc>
kubectl cordon <node>; kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets
concepts.tip: `describe` and `logs --previous` solve most problems.

concepts.what: Helm packages apps as charts with a values file. Namespaces split a cluster by team or environment. RBAC controls who can do what.
concepts.why: Rounds out the 'how do you run it in prod' answer.
concepts.ex:
helm install redis bitnami/redis -f values.yaml
helm upgrade redis bitnami/redis -f values.yaml
helm rollback redis 1
helm list -A

kubectl create namespace payments
kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n payments --as jane
concepts.tip: Honest line if pushed deep: 'I've supported the infrastructure around Kubernetes and can troubleshoot at the pod level; I haven't run clusters day to day.'

qa.q: What is Kubernetes and why use it?
qa.a: It runs containers across a cluster of machines. You declare what you want and it handles scheduling, restarts failed containers, scales, does rolling updates and gives services stable names. It replaces a lot of manual server and deployment work.

qa.q: Explain the Kubernetes architecture.
qa.a: Control plane: the API server is the front door, etcd stores cluster state, the scheduler places pods, and controllers keep actual state matching desired state. Each worker node runs the kubelet (runs pods), kube-proxy (service networking) and a container runtime like containerd.

qa.q: Pod vs container vs deployment?
qa.a: A container is one running process image. A pod wraps one or more containers that share network and storage. A Deployment manages a set of identical pods, keeps the count right and handles updates.

qa.q: What are the Service types?
qa.a: ClusterIP for internal traffic (default), NodePort to open a port on every node, LoadBalancer to get a cloud load balancer, and ExternalName to alias an outside DNS name.

qa.q: Liveness vs readiness probe?
qa.a: Liveness failing means the container is restarted. Readiness failing means the pod is taken out of the Service so it gets no traffic, but it isn't restarted.

qa.q: A pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. What do you do?
qa.a: `kubectl logs <pod> --previous` to see why the last run died, then `kubectl describe pod` for events like OOMKilled or a failed liveness probe. Common causes: bad config or missing secret, wrong command, app can't reach its database, memory limit too low, or a liveness probe that's too aggressive.

qa.q: A pod is in ImagePullBackOff. Causes?
qa.a: Wrong image name or tag, the image doesn't exist, the node can't reach the registry, or missing credentials (imagePullSecret or registry permissions). `describe pod` shows the exact error.

qa.q: A pod is stuck in Pending. Why?
qa.a: The scheduler can't place it: not enough CPU or memory for its requests, a nodeSelector or affinity no node matches, taints it doesn't tolerate, or a PVC that isn't bound. The Events in `describe pod` say which.

qa.q: A pod shows OOMKilled. What happened?
qa.a: It used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed it. Raise the limit if it's undersized, or fix the leak. Check usage with `kubectl top pod`.

qa.q: The Service exists but traffic doesn't reach the pods. What do you check?
qa.a: `kubectl get endpoints <svc>`. If empty, the Service selector doesn't match the pod labels, or the pods aren't Ready. Also check `targetPort` matches the port the container listens on, and any NetworkPolicy blocking traffic.

qa.q: ConfigMap vs Secret?
qa.a: Both inject config into pods. ConfigMaps are for plain settings. Secrets are for sensitive values, can be encrypted at rest and access-controlled separately. By default Secrets are only base64-encoded.

qa.q: Requests vs limits?
qa.a: Requests are what the scheduler reserves and uses to place the pod. Limits are the maximum. Over the CPU limit the container is throttled; over the memory limit it's killed.

qa.q: Deployment vs StatefulSet vs DaemonSet?
qa.a: Deployment for stateless, interchangeable pods. StatefulSet for apps that need stable names and their own storage, like databases. DaemonSet runs one pod per node, for agents like log shippers or monitoring.

qa.q: How does a rolling update work, and how do you roll back?
qa.a: The Deployment creates new pods and removes old ones a few at a time, controlled by maxSurge and maxUnavailable, waiting for readiness. Roll back with `kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name>`.

qa.q: cordon vs drain?
qa.a: cordon marks a node unschedulable so no new pods land on it. drain does that and also evicts the pods already there, for maintenance or patching.

qa.q: What is Helm?
qa.a: A package manager for Kubernetes. A chart is a templated set of manifests; a values file customizes it per environment. Helm tracks releases, so you can upgrade and roll back.

qa.q: How does a request from the internet reach a pod?
qa.a: DNS resolves to a cloud load balancer, which forwards to the ingress controller. The ingress controller routes by host and path to a Service. kube-proxy rules send it to one of the ready pods behind that Service.

qa.q: How do you upgrade a cluster safely?
qa.a: Read the release notes for removed APIs. Upgrade the control plane first, then node pools one at a time: cordon and drain each node, upgrade or replace it, uncordon. PodDisruptionBudgets keep enough replicas running. On AKS or EKS the provider does much of this.

qa.q: A node goes NotReady. What do you check?
qa.a: `kubectl describe node` for conditions like disk or memory pressure. On the node: kubelet status and logs, the container runtime, disk space and network. Kubernetes reschedules its pods after a timeout. Cordon it while you investigate.

qa.q: How do you secure a cluster?
qa.a: RBAC with least privilege, namespaces per team, NetworkPolicies to limit pod-to-pod traffic, no privileged containers, scanned images from a trusted registry, secrets in a vault or encrypted at rest, a private API endpoint, and staying on supported versions.

qa.q: How can you use the `startupProbe` in a pod specification to improve reliability for applications with slow initialization in Kubernetes 1.18+?
qa.a: The `startupProbe` lets you define custom checks for application startup, separate from liveness and readiness probes. This prevents premature restarts for apps that take longer to initialize. You specify the probe in the pod manifest, and Kubernetes will only start liveness and readiness checks after the startup probe succeeds.

qa.q: Describe a troubleshooting approach when a Kubernetes deployment's pods are not registering with a Service, despite matching labels and correct selector configuration. What recent networking features or settings might affect this?
qa.a: I'd check for issues with service endpoints, such as missing endpoints due to pod network policies or misconfigured `ServiceAccount` permissions. With recent versions, I'd also verify if any CNI plugin settings or network policies are blocking traffic, and inspect the `Endpoints` resource to ensure pods are listed. Features like `TopologyAwareHints` in Services can affect routing, so I'd review those settings as well.

qa.q: How can you leverage the `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` resource introduced in recent Kubernetes versions to enforce custom deployment prerequisites, such as required labels or resource limits, before pods are scheduled?
qa.a: You can define a `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` that specifies CEL (Common Expression Language) rules to check for required fields, labels, or resource constraints in deployment manifests. When users attempt to create or update resources, the policy intercepts the request and only allows it if the conditions are met, providing a flexible and declarative way to enforce organizational standards at the API level.

qa.q: How can you use the `EphemeralContainers` feature in recent Kubernetes versions to troubleshoot a running pod without restarting it?
qa.a: You can add an ephemeral container to a running pod using the `kubectl debug` command, which leverages the `EphemeralContainers` API. This allows you to run debugging tools inside the pod's network and process namespace without restarting or modifying the original containers, making it ideal for live troubleshooting.

qa.q: How can you use the `TopologySpreadConstraints` feature in recent Kubernetes versions to improve deployment resilience and availability across failure domains?
qa.a: `TopologySpreadConstraints` allow you to control how pods are distributed across different topology domains such as zones or nodes. By specifying these constraints in your deployment spec, you can ensure that pods are spread out to minimize the impact of node or zone failures, enhancing high availability. This is configured under the `spec` of a deployment or pod template using the `topologySpreadConstraints` field.

qa.q: How would you use the `PodDisruptionBudget` resource to ensure high availability during voluntary disruptions, and what recent changes should you consider when configuring it for large-scale deployments?
qa.a: I would define a `PodDisruptionBudget` (PDB) specifying either `minAvailable` or `maxUnavailable` for my deployment, ensuring a minimum number of pods remain available during node drains or voluntary disruptions. In recent Kubernetes versions, I would also consider the improvements in eviction handling and the ability to use `unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy` to better control eviction of unhealthy pods, which helps maintain service reliability in large clusters.

concepts.what: Version control. Work on a branch, commit, push, open a pull request for review, merge into main.
concepts.why: Infra code (Terraform, Ansible, configs) goes through Git like app code.
concepts.ex:
git clone https://github.com/org/infra.git
git checkout -b fix/nginx-timeout
# edit files
git add -A
git commit -m "Raise nginx proxy timeout to 60s"
git push -u origin fix/nginx-timeout
# open a pull request
git log --oneline -5
git diff main
concepts.tip: A pull request is basically a change request with automated checks.

concepts.what: CI = build and test on every commit. CD = promote the tested build through environments, with approvals where needed.
concepts.why: You'll be asked to explain CI/CD even for a non-DevOps role.
concepts.ex:
checkout → build → unit test → security scan → publish artifact
        → deploy dev → smoke test → approval → deploy prod

# .github/workflows/build.yml
on: [push]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - run: docker build -t myacr.azurecr.io/app:${{ github.sha }} .
    - run: docker push myacr.azurecr.io/app:${{ github.sha }}
concepts.tip: Your part: runners, target servers, service accounts, firewall rules, LB pools and monitoring.

concepts.what: Self-hosted CI server. Pipelines are written in a Jenkinsfile in the repo.
concepts.why: Still very common in large enterprises.
concepts.tip: 'Deploy step: connection refused' is often a firewall rule from the Jenkins agent subnet.

concepts.what: Rolling, blue/green and canary all rely on the load balancer and health checks.
concepts.why: Connects DevOps questions back to your LB strength.
concepts.ex:
Rolling     update a few servers at a time behind the LB
Blue/green  two full environments, flip the LB to the new one
Canary      send 5% of traffic to the new version, then more

Rollback:   rolling → redeploy old version
            blue/green → flip back
            canary → set weight to 0
concepts.tip: Blue/green gives the fastest rollback; it costs double the capacity.

concepts.what: Describes cloud resources in code. `plan` shows the changes, `apply` makes them. A state file tracks what exists.
concepts.why: The standard tool for creating infrastructure.
concepts.ex:
resource "azurerm_resource_group" "app" {
  name     = "rg-app-prod"
  location = "centralus"
}

terraform init
terraform plan -out tf.plan
terraform apply tf.plan
concepts.tip: Keep state in remote storage with locking so two people can't apply at once.

concepts.what: Agentless configuration over SSH or WinRM. Playbooks in YAML. Idempotent: run twice, same result.
concepts.why: Perfect for patching, baselines and user management across a fleet.
concepts.ex:
- hosts: workstations
  become: true
  tasks:
  - name: Install chrony
    ansible.builtin.apt: { name: chrony, state: present }
  - name: Disable root SSH login
    ansible.builtin.lineinfile:
      path: /etc/ssh/sshd_config
      regexp: '^PermitRootLogin'
      line: 'PermitRootLogin no'
    notify: restart ssh
  handlers:
  - name: restart ssh
    ansible.builtin.service: { name: ssh, state: restarted }

ansible-playbook site.yml -i inventory --check   # dry run
concepts.tip: Terraform creates the VM; Ansible configures what's on it.

qa.q: Explain CI/CD.
qa.a: Continuous Integration builds and tests code automatically on every commit so problems show up early. Continuous Delivery promotes a tested build through environments automatically, with approval gates where the business wants them. From infra, I make sure the runners, targets, credentials and network paths are in place and monitored.

qa.q: What is a build artifact?
qa.a: The packaged output of a build, like a JAR, a zip or a container image, stored with a version in a repository so the exact same thing goes to every environment.

qa.q: What is a pull request?
qa.a: A request to merge a branch into main, with code review and automated checks first. For infra code it works like a change request.

qa.q: Blue/green vs rolling vs canary?
qa.a: Rolling updates a few servers at a time. Blue/green runs two full environments and flips the load balancer. Canary sends a small slice of traffic to the new version first. All of them rely on the LB and health checks.

qa.q: The pipeline fails at deploy with 'connection refused'. What do you check?
qa.a: Can the build agent reach the target on that port (SSH 22, WinRM 5985/5986)? Usually a missing firewall rule from the agent subnet, the service not running on the target, or wrong credentials. Test from the agent with `nc -zv`.

qa.q: Terraform vs Ansible?
qa.a: Terraform provisions infrastructure (VMs, networks, load balancers) and tracks it in state. Ansible configures what runs on the machines. They're often used together.

qa.q: What is Terraform state and why keep it remote?
qa.a: State maps your code to real resources. Kept remote (Azure Storage, S3) with locking, the team shares one source of truth and two people can't apply at the same time and corrupt it.

qa.q: What does idempotent mean?
qa.a: Running it once or ten times leaves the system in the same state. Ansible modules check before changing; a plain shell script usually doesn't.

qa.q: Why use infrastructure as code?
qa.a: Builds are repeatable and reviewable, changes are version-controlled, environments stay identical, and rollback is reverting a commit. No hand-built snowflake servers.

qa.q: How do you handle secrets in pipelines?
qa.a: Never in the repo. Store them in a vault (Azure Key Vault, HashiCorp Vault) or the CI tool's credential store, inject them at runtime, mask them in logs, and prefer short-lived identities like OIDC or managed identities over long-lived keys.

qa.q: How would you configure a GitHub Actions workflow to ensure that a pipeline triggered by a pull request always tests the changes against the latest `main` branch, even when the workflow is re-run?
qa.a: I would use the `actions/checkout` action with the `fetch-depth: 0` and `ref: refs/heads/main` options, then merge the PR branch into `main` within the workflow using a `git merge` step. This ensures that the workflow always tests the PR changes on top of the current `main`, regardless of when the workflow is re-run.

concepts.what: Four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Three pillars: metrics, logs, traces.
concepts.why: Answer 'what would you monitor for a new app?' with these.
concepts.ex:
Latency     p95 response time under 300 ms?
Traffic     requests per second
Errors      5xx rate, failed logins
Saturation  CPU, memory, disk, connection pool

Plus host basics: up/down, disk free, cert expiry, backup success
concepts.tip: Alert on symptoms users feel (errors, latency), not on causes like CPU.

concepts.what: Pulls metrics from each target's `/metrics` endpoint on a schedule, stores them as time series, evaluates alert rules, and sends alerts to Alertmanager.
concepts.why: The most common open-source metrics stack.
concepts.ex:
# prometheus.yml
scrape_configs:
- job_name: node
  static_configs:
  - targets: ['web01:9100', 'web02:9100']

# PromQL
up == 0                                           # target down
(node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"}
  / node_filesystem_size_bytes) < 0.10            # disk < 10% free
rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])      # 5xx per second
concepts.tip: node_exporter for hosts, blackbox_exporter to probe URLs from outside.

concepts.what: A PromQL expression, how long it must be true, and a severity.
concepts.why: They may ask you to write one.
concepts.ex:
groups:
- name: host
  rules:
  - alert: HostDiskAlmostFull
    expr: (node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"}
           / node_filesystem_size_bytes) < 0.10
    for: 10m
    labels:
      severity: warning
    annotations:
      summary: "{{ $labels.instance }} root disk under 10%"
concepts.tip: `for:` stops one-off spikes from paging anyone.

concepts.what: Dashboards on top of Prometheus, Dynatrace, Azure Monitor and more.
concepts.why: 'What panels would you put on a dashboard?' is common.
concepts.ex:
Web app dashboard:
  [ Up? (blackbox) ] [ Requests/s ] [ 5xx % ] [ p95 latency ]
  [ CPU per host   ] [ Memory     ] [ Disk  ] [ LB pool health ]
  [ DB connections ] [ Cert days left                          ]
concepts.tip: Top row answers 'is it OK right now?'; detail goes below.

concepts.what: Know one line for each.
concepts.why: They'll ask what you've used and how tools compare.
concepts.ex:
Dynatrace   agent auto-instruments apps, AI root cause, APM
Datadog     SaaS agent: metrics, logs, APM, synthetics
New Relic   APM-first SaaS
Splunk      log search and SIEM, SPL queries, priced per GB
ELK         Elasticsearch + Logstash/Beats + Kibana, open source
Nagios/Zabbix  classic up/down and threshold checks
SolarWinds  network: SNMP, bandwidth, devices
Azure Monitor / CloudWatch  cloud-native metrics and logs
concepts.tip: Name the tools you have actually used and what you did with them.

concepts.t: Azure Monitor, Log Analytics and KQL
concepts.what: Azure Monitor collects platform metrics, activity logs and resource logs. Logs land in a Log Analytics workspace and are queried with KQL. The Azure Monitor Agent plus Data Collection Rules pull guest OS logs and perf counters from VMs.
concepts.why: Any Azure ops role expects basic KQL. It's the Azure equivalent of grepping logs across every server at once.
concepts.ex:
// failed requests at App Gateway in the last hour, by backend
AzureDiagnostics
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) and ResourceType == "APPLICATIONGATEWAYS"
| where httpStatus_d >= 500
| summarize count() by serverRouted_s, httpStatus_d

// VMs with low free disk
Perf
| where ObjectName == "LogicalDisk" and CounterName == "% Free Space"
| summarize min(CounterValue) by Computer, InstanceName
| where min_CounterValue < 10

// who deleted something?
AzureActivity
| where OperationNameValue endswith "DELETE"
| project TimeGenerated, Caller, ResourceGroup, _ResourceId
concepts.tip: KQL reads like a pipeline: table | where | summarize | project. Learn those four operators and `ago()` and you can answer most questions.

concepts.what: Synthetic monitoring probes the app from outside like a user (URL ping, scripted login). Alert routing sends each alert to the team that can fix it, with a runbook link.
concepts.why: 'Monitoring was green but users were down' happens when you only watch servers from the inside.
concepts.ex:
Synthetic: Dynatrace synthetic, New Relic Synthetics, Azure App Insights
           availability test, Prometheus blackbox_exporter
  check every 1-5 min from 2+ locations, alert after 2 locations fail

Every alert needs
  owner team + on-call rotation
  severity (page vs ticket)
  runbook link: what it means, first 3 checks, escalation
  a review date (delete alerts nobody acts on)
concepts.tip: An alert without an owner and a runbook is noise you've scheduled for later.

qa.q: What would you monitor for a new web application?
qa.a: The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Plus host health (CPU, memory, disk), a synthetic check from outside, load balancer pool health, certificate expiry and backup success.

qa.q: How does Prometheus collect metrics?
qa.a: It pulls. On an interval it scrapes each target's HTTP `/metrics` endpoint, found by static config or service discovery. node_exporter exposes host metrics. Because it pulls, it knows when a target is down (`up == 0`).

qa.q: Metrics vs logs vs traces?
qa.a: Metrics are numbers over time, cheap and good for alerting. Logs are detailed event records for investigation. Traces follow one request across services to show where time was spent.

qa.q: Push vs pull monitoring?
qa.a: Pull (Prometheus): the server scrapes targets, simple firewalling, detects dead targets. Push (Datadog agent, StatsD): agents send data out, which suits short-lived jobs and NAT. Prometheus uses Pushgateway for batch jobs.

qa.q: APM vs infrastructure monitoring?
qa.a: Infrastructure monitoring watches hosts and services: CPU, disk, process up. APM instruments the application itself: transaction times, slow database calls, code-level errors. Dynatrace and Datadog do both.

qa.q: How do you reduce alert noise?
qa.a: Alert on symptoms rather than causes, add `for:` durations to stop flapping, split severities (page vs ticket), group and dedupe in Alertmanager, and review alerts monthly, deleting ones nobody acts on.

qa.q: How would you centralize logs for 150 servers?
qa.a: Ship them with Filebeat, Fluent Bit or rsyslog to a central store like ELK, Splunk or Loki. Use structured JSON logs where possible, set retention by log type, and alert on patterns like auth failures or OOM kills.

qa.q: What are SLI, SLO and error budget?
qa.a: SLI is what you measure, like the share of requests under 300 ms. SLO is the target, like 99.5%. The error budget is the 0.5% you're allowed to miss; when it's used up, you slow down changes.

qa.q: Tell me about an alert you handled on call.
qa.a: Structure: what fired and when, how you triaged (dashboard → logs → host), what you did to restore service first, the root cause you found afterward, and what you changed so it won't page again: a fixed threshold, a runbook, or automation.

qa.q: A server is down at 3 a.m. Walk me through it.
qa.a: Acknowledge the page. Check monitoring: host, app or network? Use the console (vCenter, iLO) to see if the OS is alive. If it's hung, capture what you can and reboot. Verify services and LB health. Post status updates. Afterward, review logs, find the root cause and open a problem ticket.

qa.q: What is synthetic monitoring and why have it?
qa.a: Scripted probes that act like a user from outside (load the URL, log in, check the response). They catch problems server-side metrics miss: DNS, certs, LB, WAF, network path. Run them from at least two locations to avoid false alarms.

qa.q: Monitoring was all green but users said the app was down. How?
qa.a: You were watching causes (CPU, process up) not symptoms. The break was outside what you monitored: DNS, cert, LB pool, WAF, a dependency, or the network path. Fix: synthetic checks from the user's side, error-rate and latency alerts at the LB, and dependency checks.

qa.q: What is KQL and give an example you'd use?
qa.a: Kusto Query Language for Log Analytics / Azure Monitor. Example: `Perf | where CounterName == "% Free Space" | summarize min(CounterValue) by Computer | where min_CounterValue < 10` to find VMs low on disk. Pattern: table | where | summarize | project.

qa.q: What makes a good alert?
qa.a: It's actionable, tied to user impact or imminent failure, routed to the team that can fix it, has a severity and a runbook, uses a duration to avoid flapping, and gets reviewed. If nobody does anything when it fires, delete or downgrade it.

qa.q: How would you set up monitoring for a newly onboarded app?
qa.a: Agree SLOs with the owner first. Then: synthetic check on the public URL, LB metrics (5xx rate, latency, healthy members), host metrics and disk, APM agent for transactions and dependencies, log shipping with error-pattern alerts, cert expiry, backup job status. Dashboards for the app team, alerts routed to their on-call with runbooks, and a review after the first two weeks to tune noise.

qa.q: How would you use Prometheus or Grafana to monitor and alert on unauthorized AI agent behavior in a production environment?
qa.a: I would define custom metrics that track agent actions and decision boundaries, exposing them via an HTTP endpoint for Prometheus scraping. In Grafana, I'd set up dashboards to visualize anomalous activity patterns and configure alert rules that trigger when agent outputs deviate from expected ranges, leveraging Prometheus Alertmanager for notifications. This approach enables early detection of agentic drift or containment failures.

qa.q: How would you configure Prometheus and Grafana to detect and alert on lateral movement or privilege escalation attempts by AI agents within a cloud environment?
qa.a: I would define custom Prometheus exporters or use existing ones to collect audit logs and security events from cloud IAM APIs, then build Grafana dashboards to visualize anomalous access patterns, such as sudden role changes or access to sensitive resources. Alerting rules would be set up in Prometheus Alertmanager to trigger notifications on thresholds or patterns indicating lateral movement, integrating with SIEM tools for correlation.

topics.name: Cloud (Azure/AWS)
topics.blurb: Governance, hub-spoke, private endpoints, SNAT, identity, HA, cost

concepts.t: Azure building blocks and AWS equivalents
concepts.what: The same ideas with different names on each cloud.
concepts.why: Lets you answer for either cloud.
concepts.ex:
Azure                    AWS
Resource Group           (tags / CloudFormation stack)
VNet + Subnet            VPC + Subnet
NSG                      Security Group / NACL
Virtual Machine          EC2
Load Balancer (L4)       NLB
Application Gateway (L7) ALB
Azure DNS                Route 53
Entra ID + RBAC          IAM
Key Vault                Secrets Manager / KMS
Storage Account (Blob)   S3
Azure Monitor            CloudWatch
AKS                      EKS
concepts.tip: Lead with the cloud you have actually used.

concepts.what: Web, app and data tiers in separate subnets with tight rules between them.
concepts.why: Common whiteboard question.
concepts.ex:
Internet
   │ 443
[ App Gateway + WAF ]   TLS cert from Key Vault
   │
subnet-web   2 VMs in availability zones 1 and 2
   │ 8080 only
subnet-app   app VMs or AKS
   │ 1433 only
subnet-data  Azure SQL (private endpoint)

NSGs: allow only the arrows above; deny everything else
concepts.tip: Private endpoints keep databases off the public internet.

concepts.what: Managed identities let a VM or app authenticate to Azure services without a stored password. RBAC grants roles at a scope.
concepts.why: 'How do you avoid credentials in config?' is common.
concepts.ex:
az vm identity assign -g rg-app -n web01
az role assignment create \
  --assignee <principal-id> \
  --role "Key Vault Secrets User" \
  --scope /subscriptions/<sub>/resourceGroups/rg-app
concepts.tip: AWS equivalent: an IAM role attached to the EC2 instance.

concepts.what: Availability set = spread across racks in one datacenter. Availability zone = separate datacenters in a region. Region pair = disaster recovery.
concepts.why: HA questions come up in every cloud round.
concepts.ex:
Single VM (premium SSD)   99.9%
Availability set          99.95%
Availability zones        99.99%
Second region             disaster recovery
concepts.tip: Two VMs behind a load balancer across zones is the standard answer.

concepts.what: Management groups → subscriptions → resource groups → resources. RBAC and Azure Policy are inherited down the tree. A landing zone is the pre-built, governed foundation (networking, identity, policy, logging) that app teams deploy into.
concepts.why: Enterprise Azure interviews assume you know where an app 'lands' and who controls what.
concepts.ex:
Tenant Root
 └─ MG: Corp
     ├─ MG: Platform   (connectivity hub, identity, management/logging subs)
     └─ MG: LandingZones
          ├─ sub-app1-prod   rg-app1-prod-cus
          └─ sub-app1-nonprod

RBAC        WHO can do WHAT (Owner, Contributor, Reader, custom)
Policy      WHAT is allowed (allowed regions, required tags, no public IPs)
Tags        owner, costcenter, env, app  (billing + ownership)
Locks       CanNotDelete on critical resources
concepts.tip: RBAC controls people; Policy controls resources. 'Deny public IP' is Policy, not RBAC.

concepts.what: A hub VNet holds shared services (Azure Firewall, VPN/ExpressRoute gateway, Bastion, DNS resolver). Each app gets a spoke VNet peered to the hub. UDRs send spoke traffic to the firewall. On-prem connects via site-to-site VPN or ExpressRoute.
concepts.why: This is how almost every enterprise Azure tenant is built; your app onboarding lives inside it.
concepts.ex:
On-prem ==ExpressRoute/VPN== [ HUB: FW 10.0.1.4, GW, Bastion, DNS resolver ]
                                   │ peering        │ peering
                         [ SPOKE app1 ]      [ SPOKE app2 ]

UDR on spoke subnets:  0.0.0.0/0 -> 10.0.1.4 (firewall)
                       10.0.0.0/8 -> 10.0.1.4

Peering is NOT transitive: spoke1 can't reach spoke2 through the hub
unless traffic is routed through the firewall/NVA (or Virtual WAN).

VPN:          over internet, encrypted, cheaper, variable latency
ExpressRoute: private circuit, predictable latency, not encrypted by default
concepts.tip: 'Spoke-to-spoke doesn't work' = peering isn't transitive. Route via the hub firewall.

concepts.what: A private endpoint gives a PaaS service (SQL, Storage, Key Vault) a private IP in your VNet. Clients must resolve the service name to that private IP through a Private DNS zone (e.g. `privatelink.database.windows.net`) linked to the VNet, or via forwarding from on-prem DNS.
concepts.why: The #1 Azure onboarding failure: endpoint created, but the name still resolves to the public IP.
concepts.ex:
nslookup mysql01.database.windows.net
# GOOD: CNAME mysql01.privatelink.database.windows.net -> 10.60.3.4
# BAD:  resolves to a public IP -> DNS zone not linked / on-prem not forwarding

On-prem clients: conditional forwarder for database.windows.net
  -> Azure DNS Private Resolver inbound endpoint (in the hub)
  -> Azure DNS 168.63.129.16 -> private zone

Service endpoint: traffic stays on the Azure backbone, service keeps its PUBLIC IP
Private endpoint: service gets a PRIVATE IP in your VNet (preferred)
concepts.tip: `168.63.129.16` is Azure's platform IP: DNS, DHCP, LB probes, VM agent. Never block it.

concepts.what: VMs reach the internet via a NAT Gateway, a firewall, LB outbound rules, or an instance public IP. Newer subnets don't get 'default outbound access'. Each outbound path has a finite pool of SNAT ports.
concepts.why: 'Random outbound timeouts under load' in Azure is very often SNAT port exhaustion.
concepts.ex:
Options (best first)
  NAT Gateway            simple, scalable, static egress IP
  Azure Firewall         inspection + FQDN allowlists (hub)
  LB outbound rules      fine-grained port allocation
  Public IP on the VM    avoid for servers

SNAT exhaustion symptoms
  intermittent connect timeouts to ONE destination under load
  Metric: 'SNAT Connection Count' (failed) on LB / NAT GW
Fix: NAT Gateway, more public IPs, connection pooling/keep-alive in the app
concepts.tip: The app opening a new connection per request is the usual root cause. Connection reuse fixes more SNAT problems than more IPs.

concepts.t: Azure compute options for an app
concepts.what: From most control to least ops: VM → VM Scale Set → AKS → Container Apps → App Service → Functions. ACI runs single containers with no built-in LB or autoscale.
concepts.why: 'How would you host this?' depends on control vs ops effort, and you'll be asked to justify.
concepts.ex:
VM / VMSS        legacy apps, full OS control, you patch everything
AKS              many microservices, team knows Kubernetes
Container Apps   containers without running Kubernetes yourself, scale to zero
App Service      web apps/APIs (.NET, Java, Node, Python), PaaS, slots for blue/green
Functions        event-driven, short tasks
ACI              one-off/batch containers, sidecar jobs; not a prod web tier
concepts.tip: Default answer: the most managed option that meets the requirement. Then justify any step down to VMs.

concepts.t: Bastion, Key Vault and managed access
concepts.what: Azure Bastion gives RDP/SSH to private VMs through the portal or CLI without public IPs. Key Vault stores secrets, keys and certificates; access via RBAC and managed identities. Just-in-time/PIM grants admin rights only when needed.
concepts.why: Shows you build secure-by-default, not 'open 3389 to the internet'.
concepts.ex:
az network bastion ssh -g rg-hub -n bas-hub --target-resource-id <vmId> \
  --auth-type AAD
az keyvault secret show --vault-name kv-app-prod -n DbPassword
az keyvault certificate import --vault-name kv-app-prod -n app-cert -f app.pfx
concepts.tip: No public IPs on servers. Ever. Bastion or VPN in; NAT GW or firewall out.

qa.q: What is a VNet (or VPC)?
qa.a: A private network in the cloud, split into subnets, with your own IP ranges, routing and firewall rules. You can connect it to on-prem with VPN or ExpressRoute/Direct Connect.
qa.why: Cloud providers carve out a chunk of their massive network for you, isolating your resources from others by default. Subnets act like rooms in your house, each with its own address range and rules for who can enter or leave.
qa.ex:
Create a VNet:
`az network vnet create --address-prefix 10.0.0.0/16`
Add subnet:
`az network vnet subnet create --address-prefix 10.0.1.0/24`
qa.trap: Thinking VNets/VPCs are public by default; they are isolated unless you explicitly connect them.

qa.q: NSG vs Azure Firewall?
qa.a: An NSG is a free, stateful Layer 4 allow/deny list on a subnet or NIC. Azure Firewall is a paid, managed firewall with FQDN rules, threat intelligence and central logging, usually placed in a hub network.
qa.why: NSGs filter traffic at the entry and exit points of subnets or NICs, like a doorman checking IDs. Azure Firewall inspects and logs traffic centrally, like a security desk monitoring all building entrances.
qa.ex:
NSG rule:
`az network nsg rule create --priority 100 --access Allow --protocol Tcp --destination-port-range 80`
Azure Firewall FQDN rule:
`az network firewall policy rule-collection-group create --rule-type Application --target-fqdn www.microsoft.com`
qa.trap: Assuming NSGs can filter by domain names or log traffic centrally; they only filter by IP/port.

qa.q: Availability set vs availability zone?
qa.a: A set spreads VMs across fault and update domains inside one datacenter, protecting against rack failure and host maintenance. Zones spread VMs across separate datacenters in a region, with a higher SLA.
qa.why: Availability sets keep VMs apart within racks and hosts, so one hardware failure doesn't take all down. Availability zones use separate buildings, so even a datacenter outage leaves others running.
qa.ex:
Availability set:
`az vm availability-set create --platform-fault-domain-count 2`
Availability zone:
`az vm create --zone 1`
qa.trap: Confusing availability sets with zones; sets are inside one datacenter, zones are across multiple datacenters.

qa.q: How does a VM get Key Vault secrets without a stored password?
qa.a: Give the VM a managed identity and grant that identity a Key Vault role. The VM gets tokens automatically; no credentials in config files.
qa.why: The VM's managed identity acts like a badge, letting it request access tokens from Azure AD. These tokens are used to fetch secrets directly from Key Vault without ever exposing passwords.
qa.ex:
Assign managed identity:
`az vm identity assign`
Grant access:
`az keyvault set-policy --object-id <identity> --secret-permissions get`
qa.trap: Believing you need to manually store credentials or secrets on the VM; managed identity handles authentication.

qa.q: How do you patch VMs in the cloud?
qa.a: Azure Update Manager or AWS Systems Manager Patch Manager: schedules, maintenance windows and compliance reports. Or Ansible if it's hybrid with on-prem.
qa.why: Patch managers scan VMs, schedule updates, and report compliance, automating what admins used to do by hand. They use agents installed on VMs to coordinate patching without manual login.
qa.ex:
Azure Update Manager schedule:
`az automation update-management schedule create`
AWS Patch Manager:
`aws ssm create-patch-baseline`
qa.trap: Assuming cloud VMs patch themselves automatically; you must configure and schedule patching.

qa.q: Lift-and-shift vs re-platform?
qa.a: Lift-and-shift moves VMs as they are: fast, same operations. Re-platform swaps parts for managed services (SQL VM → Azure SQL, app → App Service) to cut operational work.
qa.why: Lift-and-shift copies everything as-is, like moving boxes to a new house. Re-platform replaces parts with cloud-native tools, like swapping your old fridge for a smart one after moving.
qa.ex:
Lift-and-shift:
Migrate VM with Azure Migrate.
Re-platform:
Move SQL VM to Azure SQL Database.
qa.trap: Thinking re-platform means rewriting the whole app; it just swaps infrastructure components for managed services.

qa.q: How do you control cloud cost?
qa.a: Right-size from monitoring data, auto-shutdown non-prod at night, reserved instances or savings plans for steady workloads, tag everything by owner and cost center, and set budget alerts.
qa.why: Monitoring shows which resources are oversized or idle, so you can shrink or shut them down. Tagging links costs to owners, making it clear who spends what and where.
qa.ex:
Auto-shutdown:
`az vm auto-shutdown --time 2200`
Tag resource:
`az resource tag --tags owner=alice costcenter=123`
qa.trap: Believing reserved instances always save money; they're only cost-effective for predictable, long-term workloads.

qa.q: Design a highly available web app in Azure.
qa.a: Front Door or App Gateway with WAF and a Key Vault cert, two or more web VMs or an App Service plan across availability zones, an app tier in its own subnet, Azure SQL with zone redundancy and a private endpoint, NSGs allowing only the required ports, Azure Monitor alerts plus an availability test, and backups with geo-replication for DR.
qa.why: Front Door or App Gateway routes and protects traffic before it hits your app, like a bouncer and metal detector. Spreading VMs across zones means a fire in one building doesn't stop your site.
qa.ex:
App Gateway with WAF:
`az network application-gateway create --waf-enabled true`
App Service across zones:
`az webapp create --zone 1`
qa.trap: Forgetting to use availability zones; using only availability sets leaves you vulnerable to datacenter outages.

qa.a: Azure's virtual platform IP. It provides DNS, DHCP, load balancer health probes and VM agent communication. Blocking it breaks name resolution, health probes and extensions.
qa.why: Azure uses this IP as a special endpoint inside every VNet, like a phone number for platform services. VMs rely on it for DNS lookups and agent communication, so blocking it cuts off basic functions.
qa.ex:
Ping platform IP:
`ping 168.63.129.16`
DNS server config:
`nameserver 168.63.129.16`
qa.trap: Mistaking it for a public IP or user-assigned address; it's reserved for Azure platform services only.

qa.q: Is VNet peering transitive?
qa.a: No. If A peers with hub and B peers with hub, A can't reach B through the hub by default. Route via a firewall/NVA in the hub with UDRs, peer A and B directly, or use Virtual WAN.
qa.why: Peering is like a private tunnel between two networks, not a highway hub; traffic can't hop from A to B via the hub unless you add routing or devices. Each peering is a direct connection, not a chain.
qa.ex:
A peers with hub:
`az network vnet peering create --remote-vnet hub`
B peers with hub:
`az network vnet peering create --remote-vnet hub`
A and B can't talk unless peered directly.
qa.trap: Assuming peering is transitive; by default, traffic can't flow between spokes via the hub without extra routing.

qa.q: RBAC vs Azure Policy?
qa.a: RBAC decides who can do what (a person can create VMs). Policy decides what's allowed regardless of who (VMs must have tags, no public IPs, only approved regions). They work together.
qa.why: RBAC checks the user's identity and assigned role before allowing an action, while Policy evaluates the resource's properties against rules after the action is attempted.
qa.ex:
RBAC: Assign 'Contributor' to Alice on a resource group.
Policy: Require all VMs to have 'Environment' tag.
qa.trap: Confusing RBAC and Policy as interchangeable or thinking Policy can grant permissions.

qa.q: Service endpoint vs private endpoint?
qa.a: A service endpoint keeps traffic on the Azure backbone and lets the service firewall allow your subnet, but the service keeps its public IP. A private endpoint gives the service a private IP inside your VNet, reachable from peered VNets and on-prem; it needs private DNS. Private endpoints are the enterprise default.
qa.why: A service endpoint updates the route table so traffic to the service goes over Azure's network, but the service still listens on its public IP. A private endpoint creates a network interface with a private IP in your VNet, so the service is only reachable privately.
qa.ex:
Service endpoint: Enable on subnet for 'Microsoft.Storage'.
Private endpoint: Create for 'mydb.database.windows.net', gets 10.1.2.4 in VNet.
qa.trap: Assuming service endpoints make the service private or remove its public IP.

qa.q: You created a private endpoint for Azure SQL but the app still fails or goes public. Why?
qa.a: DNS. The name must resolve to the private IP via the privatelink zone. Check `nslookup` from the app host: if it returns a public IP, the Private DNS zone isn't linked to that VNet, or the custom/on-prem DNS isn't forwarding to Azure DNS (via the DNS Private Resolver). Also check public network access is disabled on the server.
qa.why: DNS resolution for the service name must return the private endpoint's IP, or traffic will go to the public endpoint. Linking the Private DNS zone to the VNet or configuring DNS forwarding ensures the correct resolution path.
qa.trap: Thinking creating a private endpoint alone is enough without DNS configuration.

qa.q: ExpressRoute vs site-to-site VPN?
qa.a: VPN runs encrypted over the internet: quick to set up, cheaper, variable latency, lower bandwidth. ExpressRoute is a private circuit through a provider: predictable latency, higher bandwidth, SLA, more cost and lead time; not encrypted by default (add MACsec or IPsec if required). Many companies run VPN as backup to ExpressRoute.
qa.why: VPN packets travel over the public internet using IPsec encryption, while ExpressRoute uses a dedicated circuit from your site to Azure, bypassing the internet. ExpressRoute traffic is private by default but not encrypted unless you add extra layers.
qa.ex:
VPN: Site-to-site tunnel from office to Azure VNet.
ExpressRoute: MPLS circuit from provider to Azure region.
qa.trap: Believing ExpressRoute is always encrypted or that VPN and ExpressRoute are mutually exclusive.

qa.q: What is a UDR and when do you use one?
qa.a: A user-defined route overrides Azure's system routes for a subnet, typically `0.0.0.0/0` and on-prem ranges to the hub firewall's private IP so traffic is inspected. Mistakes cause black holes or asymmetric routing; check with Network Watcher next hop and effective routes.
qa.why: A UDR lets you manually set the next hop for traffic from a subnet, overriding Azure's automatic routing. This is used to force inspection or control flow, but incorrect routes can drop or misroute traffic.
qa.ex: Route 0.0.0.0/0 to 10.1.0.4 (firewall IP) in subnet's UDR.
qa.trap: Assuming Azure always routes traffic optimally without needing UDRs.

qa.q: How do admins reach private VMs without public IPs?
qa.a: Azure Bastion (RDP/SSH through the portal or `az network bastion`), a VPN/ExpressRoute from the corporate network, or a jump host. Add just-in-time access and PIM so admin rights are time-limited.
qa.why: Azure Bastion creates a managed jump box that proxies RDP/SSH over HTTPS, while VPN/ExpressRoute extends your network into Azure so you can reach private IPs directly. A jump host is a VM you connect to first, then hop to the target VM.
qa.ex: Connect to VM via Bastion in Azure Portal, or SSH from on-prem after VPN connects.
qa.trap: Thinking public IPs are required for admin access or forgetting to restrict admin access windows.

qa.q: Outbound calls from Azure VMs time out intermittently under load. What's your theory?
qa.a: SNAT port exhaustion: many short-lived connections to the same destination use up the available ports. Confirm with SNAT metrics on the LB or NAT Gateway. Fix with a NAT Gateway (or more outbound IPs) and, more importantly, connection pooling and keep-alive in the app.
qa.why: Each outbound connection from a VM to the same destination uses a unique SNAT port; under heavy load, the port pool runs out, causing dropped connections. NAT Gateway increases available ports, but reusing connections in the app is more efficient.
qa.ex: App makes 10,000 HTTP calls/sec to same API, runs out of SNAT ports, gets timeouts.
qa.trap: Blaming only network/firewall issues and not checking SNAT port usage or app connection patterns.

qa.q: What is an Azure landing zone, and how does an app team use it?
qa.a: A pre-built, governed environment: management group hierarchy, policies, a connectivity hub (firewall, gateways, DNS), central logging and identity. App teams get a subscription or spoke inside it and inherit guardrails, so they deploy fast without reinventing networking and security. Onboarding = request a landing zone, then deploy into it.
qa.why: A landing zone is a pre-configured set of resources and policies that standardizes cloud setup for teams, so they inherit security and networking controls automatically. App teams deploy into their assigned area without building the foundation themselves.
qa.ex: App team gets a new subscription under 'Corp' management group with policies and firewall already set up.
qa.trap: Thinking a landing zone is just a VNet or a template, not a governed environment with controls.

qa.q: How would you configure autoscaling for an AWS ECS Fargate service that needs to scale from zero tasks when an SQS queue receives messages, ensuring no initial capacity is wasted?
qa.a: I would use Application Auto Scaling with an SQS queue as the scaling metric, setting the minimum task count to zero and configuring a target tracking policy based on the backlog per task. To bootstrap from zero, I’d use an EventBridge rule to trigger a Lambda function that starts a task when the queue transitions from empty to non-empty, ensuring the service can scale up from zero without idle cost.

qa.q: How would you implement governance controls to ensure only approved AWS CodeConnections are used in CodePipeline workflows, given recent changes in GitHub integration security?
qa.a: I would use AWS IAM policies and AWS Organizations service control policies to restrict which CodeConnections can be referenced in CodePipeline actions. Additionally, I would leverage AWS CloudTrail and AWS Config to monitor and audit connection usage, ensuring only approved integrations are allowed and flagging unauthorized attempts.

qa.q: When configuring private endpoints for Azure PaaS services in a hub-and-spoke network, what steps ensure DNS resolution works correctly for spokes, and what pitfalls should you avoid?
qa.a: You must configure custom DNS in the spoke VNets to resolve the private endpoint's private IP, typically by forwarding requests for the service's zone to an Azure Private DNS Zone linked to the hub or central DNS. A common pitfall is forgetting to link the DNS zone to all spokes or not updating on-premises DNS, causing traffic to route publicly or fail.

qa.q: How would you enforce and monitor the use of private endpoints for all Azure PaaS resources in a multi-subscription environment, ensuring no resource is ever exposed publicly by misconfiguration?
qa.a: I would use Azure Policy with built-in and custom definitions to deny creation of PaaS resources without private endpoints and audit existing resources for public network access. Azure Defender for Cloud can alert on public exposure, and I’d configure policy assignments at the management group level to cover all subscriptions, using remediation tasks to fix non-compliant resources.

qa.q: In Azure, how would you use Managed Identities with Azure Container Apps to securely access Key Vault secrets, and what configuration is required to avoid exposing credentials?
qa.a: You assign a system-assigned or user-assigned Managed Identity to the Container App, grant it the necessary Key Vault access policy (such as `get` for secrets), and configure the app to use Azure SDKs that support Managed Identity authentication. No credentials are stored in code or configuration; the identity token is obtained via the Azure Instance Metadata Service.

topics.name: App Onboarding (End to End)
topics.blurb: Requirements, VM or container build, network, LB/TLS, monitoring, go-live, handover to the business

concepts.t: The whole lifecycle in one picture
concepts.what: Every onboarding, on-prem or Azure, VM or container, follows the same phases. Tools change; the order doesn't.
concepts.why: 'Walk me through onboarding a new application' is the question this role is built on. Say the phases in order in about 60 seconds, then go deep wherever they point.
concepts.ex:
1. Intake          owner, criticality, users, deadline, compliance
 2. Requirements    tech stack, sizing, ports/flows, NFRs (uptime, RTO/RPO, latency)
 3. Design          hosting choice, network, LB, DNS, security, DR -> architecture review
 4. Approvals       security review, firewall/LB/cert requests, CAB
 5. Provision       subnet/IPs, VMs or AKS/App Service, storage, identities (IaC)
 6. Configure       OS baseline + hardening, agents, runtime, service accounts, secrets
 7. Expose          DNS, load balancer / App Gateway, TLS cert, WAF, firewall rules
 8. Observe         monitoring, logs, synthetic checks, alerts routed with runbooks
 9. Protect         backups (restore-tested), patch group, vuln scan, DR plan
10. Validate        smoke, functional, load test, failover test, UAT by business
11. Go-live         change approved, cutover runbook, go/no-go, DNS switch
12. Hypercare       1-2 weeks of close watch, fast fixes, tune alerts
13. Handover / BAU  runbook, KT, CMDB, support model, business sign-off
concepts.tip: Interviewers listen for phases 8-13. Juniors stop at 'the server is built'. Seniors talk about who supports it at 3 a.m.

concepts.t: Intake: questions to ask the app team
concepts.what: A standard questionnaire so nothing surfaces on go-live day. Group it into business, technical, non-functional and operational.
concepts.why: Most onboarding delays are missed requirements: an outbound port nobody mentioned, an SSO integration, a compliance rule.
concepts.ex:
BUSINESS
  owner, cost center, criticality tier, go-live date
  users: internal/external, how many, where (geography, offices, VPN?)
  compliance: PCI, PII, SOX, data residency

TECHNICAL
  runtime (Java/.NET/Node/Python), OS, vendor or in-house
  CPU/RAM/disk, stateful or stateless, database type and size
  inbound ports + outbound dependencies (APIs, DBs, SaaS, file shares)
  auth: SSO (SAML/OIDC), service accounts, certificates
  batch jobs, schedules, file transfers (SFTP)

NON-FUNCTIONAL (NFRs)
  availability target (99.9? 99.99?), RTO / RPO
  peak users / requests per second, latency target
  data retention, backup frequency, DR region
  environments needed: dev / test / stage / prod

OPERATIONAL
  support team + on-call, escalation path
  deploy method (pipeline? manual?), release frequency
  maintenance / patch window, monitoring and log needs
concepts.tip: Ask for a dependency list with ports in BOTH directions. 'Outbound to partner on 8443' discovered on go-live day is the classic failure.

concepts.what: Size from data (vendor guidance, load test, current usage), not guesses. Plan for N+1, zones, growth, and naming/tagging standards.
concepts.why: Over-sizing wastes money; under-sizing causes the first outage. Panels like seeing the math.
concepts.ex:
Example
  peak 200 req/s; one instance handles ~80 req/s at 60% CPU
  200 / 80 = 2.5 -> 3 instances, +1 for N+1 = 4, split over 2 zones

Subnet sizing
  Azure reserves 5 IPs per subnet (first 4 + last)
  /27 = 32 - 5 = 27 usable
  AKS with Azure CNI: every POD takes a VNet IP -> size big (or use CNI Overlay)
  leave room to double

Environments
  dev -> test/QA -> stage (prod-like) -> prod
  stage must match prod in topology, or load tests lie

Naming / tags
  vm-app1-prod-cus-01   rg-app1-prod-cus
  tags: owner, app, env, costcenter, criticality
concepts.tip: If they don't have load numbers, say you'd start conservative, enable autoscale or quick resize, and right-size after 30 days of metrics.

concepts.what: On-prem: VMware VM (or OpenShift/K8s if the company has it). Azure: VM/VMSS, App Service, Container Apps, AKS. Pick the most managed option that meets the requirements.
concepts.why: Shows judgment, not just tool knowledge.
concepts.ex:
Question                               Points to
vendor app, needs full OS, licensing   VM (on-prem or Azure)
simple web app/API, standard runtime   App Service
containerized, few services            Container Apps
many microservices, team knows K8s     AKS / OpenShift
latency-sensitive to on-prem DB        stay near the DB (or move both)
strict data residency / site LAN    on-prem / edge

Cost of VMs you own: patching, hardening, AV/EDR, backup agents,
monitoring agents, OS upgrades every few years.
concepts.tip: Say the trade-off: 'VMs give control but my team owns patching; App Service removes that but limits OS-level access.'

concepts.t: Path A: VM build (on-prem or Azure)
concepts.what: Reserve IP/DNS → build from golden image with IaC → join domain/realm, NTP → disks/LVM → hardening → agents → patch group → service account → runtime → app deploy → systemd/IIS → local firewall → validate.
concepts.why: Say it in order with the tools.
concepts.ex:
# Azure, no public IP, zone-pinned, managed identity
az group create -n rg-app1-prod-cus -l centralus \
  --tags owner=jdoe app=app1 env=prod costcenter=1234
az vm create -g rg-app1-prod-cus -n vm-app1-prod-01 \
  --image Ubuntu2204 --size Standard_D4s_v5 --zone 1 \
  --vnet-name vnet-spoke-app1 --subnet snet-web \
  --public-ip-address "" --nsg "" \
  --assign-identity --admin-username azureadmin \
  --ssh-key-values ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

# on-prem: clone from vSphere template (or Terraform vsphere provider)
# then, same for both: Ansible
ansible-playbook baseline.yml -l vm-app1-prod-01   # CIS hardening, NTP, sssd
ansible-playbook agents.yml   -l vm-app1-prod-01   # EDR, Dynatrace, log forwarder, backup
ansible-playbook app1.yml     -l vm-app1-prod-01   # JDK, app user, systemd unit

# validate
systemctl status app1 ; ss -tlnp | grep 8080 ; curl -s localhost:8080/health
concepts.tip: In real life this is Terraform + Ansible from a pipeline. The CLI is just to show you know the parameters that matter (zone, no public IP, identity, tags).

concepts.what: Build image → scan → push to ACR → run on AKS (namespace, Deployment, Service, Ingress, probes, requests/limits, HPA, PDB) or Container Apps. Secrets from Key Vault via workload identity / CSI driver.
concepts.why: Most 'modern' onboardings are containers; you need the infra view even if devs write the manifests.
concepts.ex:
# image
az acr build -r acrcorp -t app1:1.4.0 .

# AKS (cluster normally provided by a platform team)
az aks get-credentials -g rg-aks-prod -n aks-prod
kubectl create ns app1
kubectl apply -n app1 -f deployment.yaml -f service.yaml -f ingress.yaml
kubectl get pods,svc,ingress -n app1
kubectl rollout status deploy/app1 -n app1

# OR Container Apps: no cluster to run
az containerapp up -n app1 -g rg-app1-prod \
  --image acrcorp.azurecr.io/app1:1.4.0 \
  --ingress external --target-port 8080

# ACI = single container, no LB/autoscale -> batch jobs, not a prod web tier
concepts.tip: Infra's checklist for containers: ACR access from the cluster, egress allowlists, ingress + cert, DNS, private endpoints for data, monitoring (Container Insights), and requests/limits set.

concepts.what: Build a flow matrix first. Then implement it in every place traffic is filtered: on-prem firewall, Azure Firewall, NSG, host firewall, plus routes and DNS.
concepts.why: Most onboarding delays and go-live failures are network. The flow matrix turns guesswork into a checklist.
concepts.ex:
FLOW MATRIX
Source              Destination           Port   Proto  Why
Users 10.0.0.0/8    VIP 10.50.1.10        443    TCP    app access
AppGW snet          web snet              8080   TCP    LB -> backend
web snet            SQL PE 10.60.3.4      1433   TCP    database
web snet            api.partner.com       443    TCP    via Azure FW FQDN rule
monitoring snet     web snet              9100   TCP    metrics scrape
build agents        web snet              22     TCP    deploys
web snet            on-prem AD 10.1.2.10  389/636 TCP   LDAP auth

Where each row must be allowed:
  on-prem FW -> ExpressRoute -> Azure FW (UDR) -> NSG -> host firewall
DNS: internal A/CNAME, external record if public, private DNS zone for PEs
concepts.tip: The flow matrix becomes your firewall request, your NSG rules and your troubleshooting map. Bring one to the interview as an example.

concepts.t: Exposing the app: DNS, load balancer, TLS
concepts.what: Get the cert (CSR with all SANs; internal or public CA; store in Key Vault or LB), build the VIP/listener, backend pool and health probe, then test the VIP directly before creating the DNS record.
concepts.why: Tell it as a sequence with the validation steps.
concepts.ex:
1. Cert: CSR with CN + SANs (app.example.com, app-int.example.com)
2. LB:   on-prem F5 VIP + pool + monitor + client-ssl + XFF
         Azure App Gateway: listener (443, cert from Key Vault), backend pool,
         HTTP settings, health probe (/health, 200-399), routing rule, WAF policy
3. NSG:  App Gateway v2 needs inbound 65200-65535 from GatewayManager
4. Test VIP before DNS exists:
   curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:10.50.1.10 https://app.example.com/health
   openssl s_client -connect 10.50.1.10:443 -servername app.example.com
   az network application-gateway show-backend-health -g rg -n agw-prod
5. DNS: lower TTL in advance, create/flip record at cutover
concepts.tip: Testing with `curl --resolve` before DNS means go-live is just a DNS change, and rollback is flipping it back.

concepts.what: A gate before go-live: is this app supportable, observable and recoverable by someone who isn't you?
concepts.why: This is the difference between 'it works' and 'it's production'. Panels for senior roles push on it.
concepts.ex:
[ ] Monitoring: host + APM + synthetic, dashboards shared
[ ] Alerts routed to the support team's on-call, each with a runbook
[ ] Logs shipped centrally, retention agreed
[ ] Backups configured AND a test restore done
[ ] Patch group assigned, maintenance window agreed
[ ] Vulnerability scan clean (or exceptions documented)
[ ] Certs in inventory with owner + expiry alerts
[ ] Secrets in Key Vault; service accounts documented, owners set
[ ] CMDB/ServiceNow CI created: owner, support group, dependencies
[ ] DR plan written (and tested for tier 1)
[ ] Access: who has admin, through which groups
[ ] Capacity baseline recorded
concepts.tip: Restore-tested backups is the box people skip. Say you test it.

concepts.what: Smoke → functional → integration → performance/load → resilience (kill a node) → security scan/pen test → UAT by the business.
concepts.why: The question 'how do you know it's ready?' needs more than 'the page loads'.
concepts.ex:
# quick smoke/latency loop
for i in $(seq 1 20); do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code} %{time_total}\n" https://app.example.com/health
done

# load test
k6 run --vus 200 --duration 10m load.js        # or JMeter / Azure Load Testing

# resilience: stop one backend, confirm the LB drains it and users don't notice
systemctl stop app1     (on one node)  -> watch pool health + error rate

# UAT: business users run their test cases and sign off in writing
concepts.tip: Failover test is the one most teams skip. Pulling a node in test is cheap; discovering the health check is wrong in prod isn't.

concepts.what: Approved change (CAB), a cutover runbook with timed steps and owners, a go/no-go call, communication plan, defined rollback trigger, then post-go-live validation and hypercare.
concepts.why: Shows you can run the event, not just build the server.
concepts.ex:
CUTOVER RUNBOOK (example)
T-7d   lower DNS TTL to 300; freeze config
T-1d   go/no-go: tests passed, UAT signed, rollback ready, people on bridge
T-0    20:00 bridge open, change ticket in progress
       20:05 final data sync / deploy release 1.4.0
       20:20 smoke tests against VIP (curl --resolve)
       20:30 DNS switch
       20:45 business validation
       21:00 decision point: success or ROLLBACK (flip DNS back)
T+1h   monitoring watch, comms sent
T+2w   hypercare ends -> BAU
concepts.tip: Define the rollback trigger BEFORE the window ('if X isn't working by 21:00 we roll back'). Deciding at 2 a.m. under pressure goes badly.

concepts.t: Handover to the business and support (BAU)
concepts.what: Handover is done when someone else can support the app at 3 a.m. without calling you, and the business owner has formally accepted it.
concepts.why: 'Handing over to users' is what the business actually cares about. Few candidates describe it well.
concepts.ex:
HANDOVER PACK
  architecture diagram + flow matrix
  runbook: start/stop, health checks, logs location, common issues + fixes,
           failover steps, escalation contacts (vendor, app dev, DBA, network)
  support model: L1 service desk -> L2 app support -> L3 engineering (RACI)
  monitoring: dashboard links, alert list, who gets paged
  access: AD groups for users/admins, how to request access
  SLA/SLO agreed with the business
  DR doc + last test date
  CMDB entry, known issues, open follow-up items with owners/dates

SIGN-OFF
  KT session(s) with support, recorded
  business owner signs UAT + operational acceptance
  change closed, hypercare ends, tickets now go to the support queue
concepts.tip: Make 'access for end users' explicit: AD/Entra groups, SSO app assignment, and a request process. Otherwise day one is 50 'I can't log in' tickets.

concepts.what: The same dozen problems cause most go-live pain. Knowing them makes you sound like you've done it.
concepts.why: Great material for 'tell me about a problem you hit during an onboarding'.
concepts.ex:
Health probe needs auth/redirects to SSO     -> all backends 'unhealthy'
App bound to 127.0.0.1                      -> LB can't reach it
NSG deny-all above AzureLoadBalancer rule   -> probes fail
Private endpoint, but DNS returns public IP -> zone not linked / no forwarder
Cert missing intermediate or a SAN          -> browser/Java errors
Outbound to SaaS blocked (proxy/firewall)   -> app errors only in prod
UDR to firewall one way only                -> asymmetric routing, drops
Clock skew                                  -> SSO/Kerberos failures
Service account password expired            -> app pool / service stops
No logrotate                                -> disk full on day 3
Sized by guess, no load test                -> slow at first peak
Alerts go to the build team forever         -> nobody owns it
concepts.tip: Pick two of these that really happened to you and turn them into STAR stories.

qa.q: Walk me through onboarding a new application end to end.
qa.a: Intake (owner, criticality, users, deadline), requirements and NFRs (stack, sizing, ports and dependencies, uptime, RTO/RPO), design and architecture review, approvals (security, firewall, LB, cert, CAB), provision with IaC, configure (baseline, hardening, agents, runtime, secrets), expose (DNS, LB, TLS, WAF, firewall), observe (monitoring, logs, alerts with runbooks), protect (backup with test restore, patching, vuln scan, DR), validate (smoke, load, failover, UAT), go-live with a cutover runbook and rollback trigger, hypercare, then handover with runbook, KT, CMDB and business sign-off.

qa.q: What do you need from the app team before you start?
qa.a: Owner and criticality, user base and locations, tech stack and OS, sizing, database, every inbound port and outbound dependency, authentication method, NFRs (availability, RTO/RPO, peak load, latency), environments, support team and deploy method, and the go-live date with any compliance needs.

qa.q: What are non-functional requirements?
qa.a: How the system must behave rather than what it does: availability, performance and latency, scalability, RTO/RPO, security and compliance, retention, supportability. They drive most infra decisions: zones, sizing, DR, monitoring.

qa.q: Why lower the DNS TTL before go-live?
qa.a: So clients and resolvers pick up the new record within minutes, and so a rollback (flipping the record back) takes effect quickly. Lower it a day or more ahead, since the old TTL must expire first; raise it again after.

qa.q: What goes into a runbook?
qa.a: What the app does and its dependencies, how to start/stop and check health, where logs are, common alerts and what to do, failover and recovery steps, escalation contacts, and links to dashboards and the architecture diagram. Written so on-call can act without the builder.

qa.q: How do you choose between a VM, App Service, Container Apps and AKS?
qa.a: Start with the app: vendor app needing full OS → VM. Standard web app or API → App Service. Containerized with a few services and no K8s skills → Container Apps. Many microservices and a team that runs Kubernetes → AKS. Prefer the most managed option that meets the requirements, and state who owns patching and scaling in each.

qa.q: What's a flow matrix and why build one?
qa.a: A table of every required connection: source, destination, port, protocol, purpose. It becomes the firewall and NSG requests, the security review evidence and the troubleshooting map. Building it early prevents go-live surprises.

qa.q: How do you validate a new VIP or App Gateway before go-live?
qa.a: Hit it directly with the real hostname: `curl -v --resolve app.example.com:443:<VIP> https://app.example.com/health` and `openssl s_client -servername`. Check backend health on the LB, test each backend directly with the Host header, and run a short load test. Then DNS is the only change at cutover.

qa.q: App Gateway shows every backend Unhealthy. Checklist?
qa.a: Probe path and host: does `/health` return 200-399 without auth or redirect? Is the app listening on the backend port on a non-loopback address? Do NSGs on the backend subnet allow the App Gateway subnet, and does the App Gateway subnet allow GatewayManager 65200-65535? For HTTPS backends, does the cert match the host name and is the root trusted? `az network application-gateway show-backend-health` usually tells you which.

qa.q: How do you size infrastructure for a new app?
qa.a: Use vendor guidance or current metrics, then a load test: measure what one instance handles at a safe CPU level, divide peak load by it, add N+1, and spread across zones. Size subnets for growth. Revisit after 30 days of real usage.

qa.q: What is hypercare?
qa.a: A defined period after go-live, usually one to four weeks, when the project team watches closely, fixes issues fast, tunes alerts and capacity, and answers support. It ends with a formal transition to BAU support.

qa.q: What does operational readiness mean to you?
qa.a: The app can be supported and recovered by someone other than the builder: monitoring and alerts routed with runbooks, central logs, backups with a test restore, patching assigned, vuln scan clean, certs inventoried, secrets in a vault, CMDB updated, DR documented, and the support team trained.

qa.q: How do you handle secrets and service accounts during onboarding?
qa.a: Prefer managed identities (Azure) or gMSAs (Windows) so there's no password. Anything else goes in Key Vault/Vault, injected at runtime, with an owner, rotation and monitoring. Never in config files, images or tickets.

qa.q: How do end users actually get access at go-live?
qa.a: Through groups, not individuals: AD/Entra security groups mapped to app roles, SSO app assignment if it's SAML/OIDC, a documented request/approval process, and the URL published. Test with a normal user account, not an admin, before go-live.

qa.q: The business wants go-live Friday; the load test isn't done. What do you do?
qa.a: State the risk plainly and in writing: what could happen and its impact. Offer options: a quick reduced load test, go-live with limited users, extra capacity plus close monitoring, or a short delay. If they choose to proceed, get the business owner's documented risk acceptance in the change record and plan the test as a follow-up. Don't silently comply and don't just block.

qa.q: Design onboarding for an external-facing app in Azure that depends on an on-prem database.
qa.a: Front Door (or App Gateway) with WAF and a Key Vault cert at the edge; app in a spoke VNet across zones; spoke peered to a hub with Azure Firewall and ExpressRoute to on-prem; UDRs through the firewall; on-prem firewall rules for the DB port from the app subnet only. Flag latency: a chatty app over ExpressRoute can be slow, so measure round trips early or plan to move the DB. Private endpoints for PaaS, monitoring and DR on top.

qa.q: How would you cut onboarding time from weeks to days?
qa.a: Standardize: an intake form that captures everything once, Terraform modules for VM/App Gateway/DNS/NSG patterns, Ansible roles for baseline and agents, pre-approved standard changes for the common pattern, a self-service catalog item that triggers the pipeline, and policy-as-code for guardrails. Measure lead time before and after and attack the slowest step, usually cross-team approvals.

qa.q: Halfway through a go-live, the smoke test fails. What do you do?
qa.a: Follow the runbook: check against the pre-agreed rollback trigger. If it's a quick, understood fix inside the window, fix and retest; if not, roll back (flip DNS or LB back), confirm the old service works, communicate, and close the change as failed with the reason. Then a short review before rescheduling.

qa.q: What makes the business willing to sign off?
qa.a: Their UAT cases pass, performance meets the agreed NFRs, users can actually log in with their own accounts, support knows how to handle tickets, and they have the runbook, SLA and escalation path in hand. Get acceptance in writing; it closes the project and moves ownership to BAU.

topics.name: Troubleshooting: Connectivity, Latency, Throughput
topics.blurb: A repeatable method, Linux/Windows tools, Azure Network Watcher, on-prem path

concepts.what: Define → scope → reproduce → walk the layers → split the path in half → compare working vs broken → change one thing → verify → document.
concepts.why: Panels grade the method more than the answer. A calm, structured approach beats a lucky guess.
concepts.ex:
DEFINE   what exactly fails? error text? since when? what changed?
SCOPE    one user / one site / everyone? one server / all backends?
         internal and external? only big requests?
REPRODUCE from the client's network if you can
LAYERS   DNS -> route -> port reachable -> TLS -> HTTP -> app -> dependency
SPLIT    test from the middle: LB to backend, backend to DB
COMPARE  working client vs broken client; yesterday vs today
CHANGE   one variable at a time, with evidence
VERIFY   from the user's side, not just the server
DOCUMENT timeline + root cause + fix + prevention
concepts.tip: First question out loud: 'What changed?' Half of all incidents are a recent change.

concepts.what: Bandwidth = size of the pipe. Throughput = what you actually get. Latency = round-trip time (RTT). Packet loss = packets that never arrive. Jitter = variation in latency.
concepts.why: Mixing these up in an answer is an instant credibility hit.
concepts.ex:
Bandwidth-delay product (BDP) = bandwidth x RTT
  1 Gbps x 60 ms = 7.5 MB must be 'in flight' to fill the pipe
  -> a single TCP stream needs a 7.5 MB window or it can't reach 1 Gbps

Loss hurts TCP badly (rough Mathis rule):
  throughput <= MSS / (RTT x sqrt(loss))
  1460 B, 50 ms RTT, 1% loss -> only ~2-3 Mbps per stream, on any size link

Latency per stage (rough)
  same rack < 0.5 ms   same region ~1-2 ms   DFW<->Virginia ~30-40 ms
  US<->Europe ~80-120 ms
concepts.tip: 'Upgrade the bandwidth' doesn't fix latency or loss. Say that and you'll stand out.

concepts.t: Read the error before running tools
concepts.what: The error message tells you the layer.
concepts.why: Saves ten minutes of random commands.
concepts.ex:
Could not resolve host / NXDOMAIN   -> DNS
No route to host                     -> routing / ARP / host down (ICMP unreachable)
Connection timed out                 -> packets DROPPED: firewall, NSG, routing, host down
Connection refused                   -> host reached, nothing listening (or REJECT/RST)
Connection reset by peer             -> something sent RST mid-stream: app crash, FW, LB idle timeout
SSL: certificate verify failed        -> chain / CA trust / name mismatch
HTTP 502/503/504                     -> proxy reached, backend problem
Works, but slow                      -> latency/throughput: time each phase
concepts.tip: Timeout = something silently dropped it. Refused = you reached the host. That one distinction answers many interview questions.

concepts.what: Same ladder on both OSes: interface → gateway → DNS → port → listener → firewall → packets.
concepts.why: You'll be asked to do it on whichever OS they run.
concepts.ex:
Step              Linux                         Windows
IP/interface      ip -br a                      ipconfig /all
route             ip route get <dst>            Find-NetRoute -RemoteIPAddress <dst>
DNS               getent hosts / dig            Resolve-DnsName <name>
port reachable    nc -zv <dst> 443              Test-NetConnection <dst> -Port 443
