path              traceroute -T -p 443 / mtr    tracert / pathping
HTTP/TLS          curl -v https://...           curl.exe -v https://...
listening         ss -tlnp                      Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen
local firewall    firewall-cmd / ufw / nft      Get-NetFirewallRule / wf.msc
packets           tcpdump -nni any port 443     pktmon / Wireshark
concepts.tip: Test from the actual source machine. 'It works from my laptop' proves nothing about the server's path.

concepts.t: Latency: find which phase is slow
concepts.what: Break a request into DNS, TCP connect, TLS, time-to-first-byte and transfer. Whichever phase is big is where to look.
concepts.why: Turns 'it's slow' into a specific team and a specific fix.
concepts.ex:
curl -o /dev/null -s -w 'dns %{time_namelookup}\nconnect %{time_connect}\ntls %{time_appconnect}\nttfb %{time_starttransfer}\ntotal %{time_total}\n' https://app.example.com/

# values are cumulative seconds
dns big           -> resolver slow / timeouts to first DNS server
connect big       -> network RTT, or SYN retransmits (loss/drops)
tls big           -> handshake/OCSP/CRL, cert chain, CPU on LB
ttfb big          -> backend/app/database slow (check APM, LB backend time)
total-ttfb big    -> transfer: bandwidth, window size, loss

mtr -rwc 200 app.example.com   # loss/latency per hop over time

Times clustering near 1s, 3s, 7s = TCP SYN retransmits = packets being dropped.
concepts.tip: Loss shown at a middle hop in mtr but not at the destination is usually just a router de-prioritizing ICMP. Only loss that continues to the last hop is real.

concepts.t: Throughput: why is the transfer slow?
concepts.what: Measure the network alone with iperf3, then compare single-stream vs parallel streams, check errors/MTU, and rule out disk and CPU.
concepts.why: 'File copy between datacenters is slow on a 10 Gbps link' is a common senior question.
concepts.ex:
# server side
iperf3 -s
# client side
iperf3 -c 10.2.0.11 -t 30            # one TCP stream
iperf3 -c 10.2.0.11 -t 30 -P 8       # 8 parallel streams
iperf3 -c 10.2.0.11 -t 30 -R         # reverse direction

Parallel MUCH faster than single -> latency/window limited (BDP), not bandwidth
Both slow                       -> real bandwidth cap, shaping, loss, bad link

ip -s link show eth0     # errors/drops on the NIC
ethtool eth0             # speed/duplex (100/half = mismatch)
ss -ti dst 10.2.0.11     # rtt, retrans, cwnd per connection
nstat -az | grep -i retrans
ping -M do -s 1472 10.2.0.11    # MTU 1500 path test (Linux)
ping -f -l 1472 10.2.0.11       # same on Windows

Also: disk (iostat), encryption CPU (scp is single-threaded),
Azure VM size network cap, accelerated networking off
concepts.tip: Copy is slow but iperf3 is fast = not the network. Check disk and the copy tool before opening a network ticket.

concepts.t: Packet captures: what to look for
concepts.what: Capture on both ends at the same time, filtered narrowly, and look for the handshake, resets, retransmissions and TLS alerts.
concepts.why: A capture ends the 'network vs app' argument with evidence.
concepts.ex:
tcpdump -nni any host 10.2.0.11 and port 443 -w /tmp/c.pcap   # Linux
pktmon start --capture --pkt-size 0 ; pktmon stop               # Windows
pktmon etl2pcap PktMon.etl

In Wireshark
  tcp.flags.syn==1 && tcp.flags.ack==0      SYNs (any without SYN-ACK = dropped)
  tcp.flags.reset==1                        who sends RST? server, LB or firewall?
  tcp.analysis.retransmission               loss
  tcp.analysis.zero_window                  receiver can't keep up (app/host slow)
  tls.alert_message                         TLS failure reason

SYN seen leaving client, not arriving at server -> something in between drops it
concepts.tip: Seeing the SYN leave the client but never arrive at the server is the clearest proof a firewall/NSG/route is the problem.

concepts.what: Network Watcher answers 'would this be allowed and where would it go?' without guessing: IP flow verify, NSG diagnostics, next hop, effective routes, effective security rules, connection troubleshoot, packet capture, flow logs.
concepts.why: In Azure you can't plug into a switch. These tools are how you prove where traffic dies.
concepts.ex:
# would the NSG allow it?
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg --vm vm-web01 --direction Inbound \
  --protocol TCP --local 10.60.1.4:8080 --remote 10.60.0.5:50000

# where does traffic go next? (UDR to firewall? None = black hole)
az network watcher show-next-hop -g rg --vm vm-web01 \
  --source-ip 10.60.1.4 --dest-ip 10.10.5.20

# what rules/routes actually apply to the NIC
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g rg -n vm-web01-nic
az network nic show-effective-route-table -g rg -n vm-web01-nic -o table

# end-to-end test from the VM
az network watcher test-connectivity -g rg --source-resource vm-web01 \
  --dest-address sql01.database.windows.net --dest-port 1433

# run a command inside the VM without SSH
az vm run-command invoke -g rg -n vm-web01 --command-id RunShellScript \
  --scripts "ss -tlnp; curl -sv localhost:8080/health"

az network application-gateway show-backend-health -g rg -n agw-prod

Also: VNet/NSG flow logs + Traffic Analytics, Connection Monitor,
Azure Firewall logs (KQL), Boot diagnostics + Serial console,
Resource Health / Service Health (is it Azure?)
concepts.tip: Order in Azure: Resource Health → effective NSG + IP flow verify → next hop/effective routes → firewall logs → DNS (private zones) → inside the VM.

concepts.what: Things that behave differently from on-prem.
concepts.why: These are the 'have you actually run Azure?' questions.
concepts.ex:
ICMP is often blocked; test with TCP (nc / Test-NetConnection), not ping
168.63.129.16 must be reachable (DNS, probes, agent)
NSGs are stateful; Azure Firewall too, so asymmetric routes get dropped
Peering isn't transitive; spoke-to-spoke needs the hub FW + UDRs
New subnets may have no default outbound internet -> NAT Gateway/FW
SNAT port exhaustion -> intermittent outbound timeouts under load
Private endpoint + wrong DNS = traffic tries the public IP and fails
VM size caps network bandwidth; accelerated networking matters
LB idle timeout default ~4 min -> long idle connections get dropped; use TCP keepalives
concepts.tip: If on-prem works and Azure doesn't, check DNS and routes before NSGs. They're the two things that differ most.

concepts.t: On-prem path and who to engage
concepts.what: Client → access switch → core → firewall → load balancer → server (VLAN/port group) → storage/DB. Gather evidence per hop before escalating.
concepts.why: In big companies you often don't own every hop. Bringing the right evidence to the right team is the senior skill.
concepts.ex:
Hop            Evidence you collect / ask for
Client/site    ipconfig, Test-NetConnection, which site/VPN, Wi-Fi vs wired
Switch         interface errors/CRC, duplex, VLAN (ask network team)
Firewall       traffic log for src/dst/port: allowed? denied? no hit?
F5 / LB        tmsh show ltm pool, VIP stats, tcpdump -ni 0.0:nnn
VMware         vNIC connected? right port group/VLAN? host uplink errors?
Server         ss/netstat, host firewall, app logs
DNS            which server answered, what record, TTL

Escalation note template:
  'From 10.1.2.3 to 10.4.5.6:443, SYN leaves client (pcap attached),
   never reaches server (pcap attached), started 14:05 after CHG123.
   Please check FW policy between zones X and Y.'
concepts.tip: A ticket with source, destination, port, time and captures gets fixed in an hour. 'App is down, please check network' sits in a queue.

concepts.what: Short starting plans for the questions you'll most likely get.
concepts.why: Having a first three steps ready keeps you calm in the room.
concepts.ex:
'App is slow for everyone'
  LB latency + 5xx per backend -> one bad node? -> host USE checks -> DB waits -> recent change
'Slow only for one site'
  traceroute/mtr from that site, WAN link utilization, proxy at that site, DNS server they use
'Intermittent timeouts'
  correlate by time: LB idle timeout? SNAT? one bad backend? GC pauses? DNS server failing?
'Works from A, not from B'
  diff the paths: source subnet firewall rules, routes, NAT, proxy, DNS view
'Moved app to Azure, DB stayed on-prem, now slow'
  chatty: 400 queries x 35 ms RTT = 14 s; co-locate app and DB
'Large uploads fail, small ones work'
  MTU/fragmentation over VPN, WAF/LB body-size limit, proxy timeout
concepts.tip: Chatty-app math (queries x RTT) is a great answer because it proves no bandwidth upgrade will help.

qa.q: Connection refused vs connection timed out?
qa.a: Refused: the host answered with a RST, so the network path works but nothing is listening on that port (or a firewall actively rejects). Timed out: no answer at all, packets are being dropped by a firewall/NSG, a routing problem, or the host is down.

qa.q: Latency vs bandwidth vs throughput?
qa.a: Bandwidth is the capacity of the link. Throughput is what you actually achieve. Latency is the time for a round trip. A high-bandwidth link can still give low throughput if latency or packet loss is high.

qa.q: How do you test whether a port is open from Linux and from Windows?
qa.a: Linux: `nc -zv host 443` (or `curl -v telnet://host:443`). Windows: `Test-NetConnection host -Port 443`. Run it from the actual source machine.

qa.q: Ping fails but the website works. How?
qa.a: ICMP is blocked by a firewall or NSG, or the host doesn't answer ping, while TCP 443 is allowed. Ping is not a valid reachability test in many networks, especially cloud. Test the real port instead.

qa.q: What does traceroute show, and what are its limits?
qa.a: The routers along the path and the latency to each. Limits: many devices drop or de-prioritize ICMP/UDP probes, so you see stars or fake loss; the return path may differ; firewalls may block it. Use TCP traceroute (`traceroute -T -p 443`) or mtr for better data.

qa.q: How do you approach 'the application is slow'?
qa.a: Clarify who, since when, all or some users, what changed. Time the request phases with curl -w (DNS, connect, TLS, TTFB, transfer). Check LB metrics per backend, host USE metrics, APM for slow transactions and DB calls, and the network path with mtr. Narrow by elimination and back every conclusion with data.

qa.q: Users at one site can't reach the app; everyone else can. Where do you look?
qa.a: Something specific to that site: its DNS servers, proxy, WAN/VPN link, a firewall rule for its subnet, or routing. Test from a machine at that site (Test-NetConnection, tracert, nslookup) and compare to a working site.

qa.q: Find which part of an HTTPS request is slow.
qa.a: `curl -o /dev/null -s -w` with time_namelookup, time_connect, time_appconnect, time_starttransfer and time_total. Big DNS = resolver; big connect = network/loss; big TLS = handshake/cert/LB CPU; big TTFB = backend; big after TTFB = transfer/bandwidth.

qa.q: A 10 Gbps link between datacenters only gives 300 Mbps on a file copy. Why?
qa.a: Test with iperf3: if parallel streams are much faster than one, a single TCP stream is limited by the window vs bandwidth-delay product, made worse by any loss. If iperf3 is fast, the bottleneck is disk or the copy tool (scp is single-threaded and encrypts). Also check NIC errors, MTU, shaping and VM network caps.

qa.q: Intermittent timeouts every few minutes. Ideas?
qa.a: Correlate timing. Candidates: one unhealthy backend in rotation, LB or firewall idle timeouts killing long-lived connections, SNAT port exhaustion under load, a failing DNS server in the resolver list, GC pauses or connection pool exhaustion in the app. LB logs per backend and packet captures narrow it quickly.

qa.q: An Azure VM can't reach an on-prem server. Walk through it.
qa.a: DNS resolves correctly? Effective NSG on the NIC and subnet (IP flow verify). Next hop: does the UDR send it to the hub firewall, and does the firewall allow and log it? Gateway/ExpressRoute up with the route advertised? On-prem firewall allows the Azure subnet? Return route from on-prem back to Azure? Test with `test-connectivity` and a capture on both sides.

qa.q: What do you look for in a packet capture?
qa.a: Whether the handshake completes (SYN without SYN-ACK = dropped), who sends RSTs, retransmissions (loss), zero-window (receiver overloaded), TLS alerts, and timing gaps between request and response that show where time is spent. Capture both ends to see where packets vanish.

qa.q: What are symptoms of an MTU problem?
qa.a: Small requests and the TCP handshake work, but large responses, file transfers or TLS handshakes with big certs hang. Common over VPNs and tunnels. Test with `ping -M do -s 1472` (Linux) or `ping -f -l 1472` (Windows) and reduce until it passes; fix with the right MTU or MSS clamping.

qa.q: How do you tell whether a slow app is the network or the application?
qa.a: Time-to-first-byte vs connect time: if TCP connect is fast but TTFB is slow, the network delivered the request quickly and the server took the time. Confirm with LB logs (request time vs backend time), APM traces and a capture showing the gap between request and response on the server side.

qa.q: What are the first Azure tools you use for a connectivity issue?
qa.a: Resource Health, then Network Watcher: effective security rules and IP flow verify (NSG), next hop and effective routes (UDR/firewall), connection troubleshoot (end to end), then Azure Firewall logs in Log Analytics, and DNS checks for private endpoints. `az vm run-command` or Serial Console to look inside the VM.

qa.q: Outbound connections from Azure fail intermittently under load. Explain.
qa.a: Likely SNAT port exhaustion: each outbound connection to the same destination IP and port uses a SNAT port from a limited pool. Short-lived connections without reuse burn through it. Confirm with SNAT metrics on the LB or NAT Gateway, fix with NAT Gateway or more public IPs, and push the app to use connection pooling and keep-alive.

qa.q: An app moved to Azure, its database stayed on-prem, and pages got 10x slower. Why and what do you do?
qa.a: Latency multiplied by chattiness: each page makes hundreds of sequential DB calls, and each now pays ExpressRoute RTT instead of LAN RTT. Bandwidth isn't the issue. Show the math, then fix by moving the database (or a replica/cache) next to the app, or have the app team batch queries.

qa.q: A single TCP transfer gets 50 Mbps on a 1 Gbps link with 80 ms RTT. Explain.
qa.a: Throughput per stream is roughly window / RTT. 50 Mbps x 0.08 s ≈ 500 KB in flight, so the effective window is about 500 KB. Filling 1 Gbps at 80 ms needs about 10 MB. Fix with TCP window scaling and buffer tuning, parallel streams, or a WAN-optimized tool; also check for loss, which collapses the window.

qa.q: The network and app teams blame each other. How do you settle it?
qa.a: Evidence, not opinions. Simultaneous captures on client and server, timing breakdown with curl -w, LB logs showing backend response time, and a timeline of changes. If the SYN leaves and never arrives, it's the path; if the request arrives quickly and the response is slow, it's the server or app. Share the data neutrally.

qa.q: Users get 'connection reset' after a few minutes of inactivity. Cause?
qa.a: An idle timeout on a firewall, NAT or load balancer (Azure LB defaults to about 4 minutes) drops the connection state; the next packet gets a RST. Fix with TCP keepalives or app-level heartbeats shorter than the timeout, or raise the idle timeout where supported.

concepts.what: ESXi hosts run VMs; vCenter manages them. Key features: vMotion, HA, DRS, templates, snapshots.
concepts.why: Core vocabulary for any on-prem virtualization role.
concepts.ex:
vMotion          move a running VM to another host, no downtime
Storage vMotion  move its disks to another datastore, no downtime
HA               host dies → its VMs restart on other hosts
DRS              balances load across hosts automatically
Templates        golden image to clone new VMs from
Customization spec  sets hostname, IP, domain join at clone time
concepts.tip: HA restarts VMs (short outage). Fault Tolerance keeps a live copy (no outage).

concepts.what: A snapshot is a point-in-time delta on the same datastore. A backup is a separate copy on different storage.
concepts.why: Asked to check you know snapshots aren't backups.
concepts.ex:
Snapshot: quick rollback before patching
  - grows over time and slows the VM
  - lost if the datastore is lost
  - delete within a few days

Backup: Veeam, Commvault, Azure Backup
  - separate storage, retention policy
  - test restores regularly
concepts.tip: Old snapshots are a common cause of slow VMs and full datastores.

concepts.what: The few metrics that explain most slow VMs.
concepts.why: 'The VM is slow but the host looks fine' is a classic.
concepts.ex:
CPU ready > 5%     VM is waiting for a physical core
Ballooning/swap    host is short on memory
Datastore latency > 20 ms   storage is the bottleneck
Long snapshot chain         every read walks the chain
Too many vCPUs     harder to schedule, can be slower
concepts.tip: Right-sizing down often fixes performance.

concepts.what: DAS = local disks. NAS = file shares over the network. SAN = block storage over Fibre Channel or iSCSI.
concepts.why: Basic storage vocabulary for any infra role.
concepts.ex:
NAS   NFS / SMB shares       file-level   Isilon, NetApp
SAN   FC / iSCSI LUNs        block-level  VMFS datastores

RAID 0   stripe, no redundancy
RAID 1   mirror
RAID 5   stripe + parity, survives 1 disk
RAID 6   double parity, survives 2 disks
RAID 10  mirror + stripe, fast, 50% capacity

IOPS = operations/sec   throughput = MB/s   latency = ms per op
concepts.tip: Databases care about IOPS and latency; backups care about throughput.

concepts.what: RPO = how much data you can lose. RTO = how fast you must be back.
concepts.why: Any DR question starts with RPO and RTO.
concepts.ex:
RPO 15 min → back up or replicate at least every 15 min
RTO 1 hour → failover must finish within 1 hour

3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 types of media, 1 offsite
Immutable backups: can't be changed or deleted (ransomware)
concepts.tip: If you've run a DR failover test, mention it here.

qa.q: Snapshot vs backup?
qa.a: A snapshot is a quick point-in-time delta on the same storage, good for rolling back a patch, but it grows, slows the VM and is lost with the datastore. A backup is a separate copy on different storage with retention. Snapshots aren't backups.

qa.q: What is vMotion?
qa.a: Live migration of a running VM from one host to another with no downtime. It needs shared storage (or storage vMotion) and compatible CPUs.

qa.q: SAN vs NAS?
qa.a: NAS shares files over the network (NFS, SMB). SAN presents block storage (LUNs) over Fibre Channel or iSCSI, and the server sees it as a raw disk.

qa.q: HA vs DRS?
qa.a: HA restarts VMs on other hosts when a host fails. DRS moves running VMs between hosts with vMotion to balance load.

qa.q: A VM is slow but the host looks fine. What do you check?
qa.a: CPU ready time, memory ballooning or swapping, datastore latency, snapshot chain length, VMware Tools version, and whether the VM has too many vCPUs.

qa.q: Thin vs thick provisioning?
qa.a: Thin allocates space as data is written, which saves space but risks overcommitting the datastore. Thick reserves all space upfront, predictable and safer for databases.

qa.q: Explain RAID 5 vs RAID 10.
qa.a: RAID 5 stripes data with parity and survives one disk failure; good capacity, slower writes and slow rebuilds. RAID 10 mirrors and stripes; fast, survives one disk per mirror pair, but you only get 50% capacity.

qa.q: What are RPO and RTO?
qa.a: RPO is how much data loss is acceptable, which sets backup or replication frequency. RTO is how quickly the service must be restored.

qa.q: How do you know your backups actually work?
qa.a: Scheduled restore tests: restore real files and full VMs to an isolated network and check the app comes up. Monitor job success, keep an offsite and an immutable copy, and document restore steps. A backup you haven't restored is only a hope.

concepts.what: Baseline settings every server should have.
concepts.why: 'How do you harden a new server?' is common.
concepts.ex:
Linux
  no root SSH, key-only auth, firewall default deny
  SELinux enforcing, auditd, minimal packages
  NTP, central logging, sudo with logging

Windows
  separate admin accounts, LAPS for local admin
  disable SMBv1 and NTLMv1, firewall on
  Defender/EDR, GPO password + lockout policy
  RDP only through a jump host with NLA
concepts.tip: CIS benchmarks are the industry standard to point to.

concepts.what: Fix what's exposed and exploitable first.
concepts.why: 'The scan shows 200 criticals' is a realistic question.
concepts.ex:
1. Internet-facing systems
2. Known exploited (CISA KEV list)
3. CVSS score
4. Group by fix: one patch can clear 50 findings
5. Waves through change management
6. Exceptions documented with a compensating control and an end date
concepts.tip: Show you think about risk, not just counts.

concepts.what: Standard changes are pre-approved and low risk. Normal changes go to CAB. Emergency changes fix an active outage and get reviewed afterward.
concepts.why: Enterprise interviews always ask about change control.
concepts.ex:
Every change request has:
  what and why
  when (window) and who
  exact steps
  validation steps
  rollback steps
  risk and blast radius
  communication plan
concepts.tip: A change without a rollback plan isn't ready.

concepts.what: Incident = restore service now. Problem = find and fix the root cause so it doesn't happen again.
concepts.why: ITIL vocabulary comes up in enterprise interviews.
concepts.ex:
Sev 1  full outage, major business impact, all hands
Sev 2  serious degradation
Sev 3  minor, workaround exists
Sev 4  cosmetic

Postmortem: timeline, impact, root cause,
            contributing factors, action items. Blameless.
concepts.tip: Restore first, investigate second.

concepts.what: Zero trust: never trust the network location; verify every request (identity, device, context), least privilege, assume breach. Secrets belong in a vault, not in code, images or wikis.
concepts.why: Security questions in infra rounds are mostly about identity and secrets now, not firewalls alone.
concepts.ex:
Secrets
  Key Vault / HashiCorp Vault / CyberArk
  managed identities / gMSA instead of passwords
  rotate; alert on use from unexpected places
  scan repos for leaked keys (GitHub secret scanning, gitleaks)

Identity
  SSO (SAML/OIDC) via Entra ID / PingFederate
  MFA everywhere, conditional access
  PIM / just-in-time admin, separate admin accounts

Network
  segmentation, private endpoints, WAF, mTLS between services
concepts.tip: If a secret was ever committed to Git, it's compromised. Rotate it; deleting the commit isn't enough.

concepts.what: Public CA certs for internet-facing names, internal (enterprise) CA for internal names. Certs have an owner, an expiry and a renewal method. mTLS means both sides present certs.
concepts.why: Cert expiry is one of the most common self-inflicted outages.
concepts.ex:
Inventory: name, SANs, issuer, expiry, where installed (LB, web, app, Java keystore), owner
Renew:     ACME (Let's Encrypt / internal ACME), Key Vault auto-renew, CA portal
Java apps: import CA into the truststore
  keytool -importcert -alias corp-root -file root.crt -keystore $JAVA_HOME/lib/security/cacerts
Check:     openssl x509 -in app.crt -noout -enddate
concepts.tip: 'PKIX path building failed' in a Java app = the JVM truststore doesn't trust the issuing CA.

qa.q: What is least privilege?
qa.a: Every person and system gets only the access it needs, only for as long as needed. Done with RBAC, groups instead of individual grants, regular access reviews, and PAM tools for admin access.

qa.q: Incident vs problem?
qa.a: An incident is restoring service as fast as possible. A problem is finding and fixing the root cause so the incident doesn't repeat.

qa.q: Describe your change process.
qa.a: Standard changes are pre-approved for routine low-risk work. Normal changes go to CAB with steps, testing, rollback, risk and a window. Emergency changes handle active outages and get reviewed afterward. I present changes at CAB, answer blast-radius questions and close the ticket with the outcome.

qa.q: Someone asks for root or local admin to 'make it easier'. What do you do?
qa.a: Find out what they actually need to do and grant only that: a sudoers rule for one command, a group membership, or a service account with specific rights. Document it.

qa.q: How do you manage service accounts?
qa.a: One per app, no interactive login, long random passwords or managed accounts (gMSA, managed identity), an owner on record, rotation, and monitoring for use from unexpected hosts.

qa.q: A change failed in production. What now?
qa.a: Run the rollback plan right away, confirm service is restored, communicate, then do a review: why did testing miss it and what changes in the process.

qa.q: What is a blameless postmortem?
qa.a: A write-up of timeline, impact, root cause, contributing factors and action items that focuses on systems and process, not on who made the mistake. People stay honest, so you actually learn.

qa.q: A vulnerability scan shows 200 critical findings. Where do you start?
qa.a: Internet-facing systems first, then anything with a known exploit, then by CVSS. Group findings by fix, since one patch often clears dozens. Schedule waves through change management, and document exceptions with a compensating control and a date.

qa.q: A critical zero-day is announced (like Log4j). Walk through your response.
qa.a: Find exposure with software inventory, package queries and the scanner. Prioritize internet-facing systems. Apply the patch or vendor mitigation, verify, and track progress. Send regular status updates, and document everything for the postmortem.

qa.q: What is MFA and why isn't a password enough?
qa.a: Multi-factor authentication requires two of: something you know, have, or are. Passwords get phished, reused and leaked; a second factor stops most account takeovers.

qa.q: What is a WAF?
qa.a: A web application firewall inspects HTTP traffic and blocks attacks like SQL injection, XSS and bad bots, usually with OWASP rule sets. It sits on an L7 device: App Gateway, Front Door, F5 ASM, Cloudflare.

qa.q: What is zero trust?
qa.a: Don't trust anything because it's on the internal network. Verify every request by identity, device and context, give least privilege, segment the network, and assume breach so you log and monitor everything.

qa.q: A password was committed to a Git repo. What do you do?
qa.a: Treat it as compromised: rotate it immediately, check logs for misuse, then remove it from history (and know that forks and clones may still have it). Move the secret to a vault and add secret scanning to the repo.

qa.q: A Java app says 'PKIX path building failed'. What does it mean?
qa.a: The JVM doesn't trust the certificate chain the server presented, usually because the internal or intermediate CA isn't in its truststore. Import the CA into the truststore the app actually uses (cacerts or a custom keystore) and restart. Don't disable validation.

qa.q: How do you prevent certificate-expiry outages across an enterprise?
qa.a: Central inventory discovered by scanning endpoints, not just by spreadsheet. An owner per cert. Automate renewal (ACME, Key Vault auto-renew) wherever possible. Alerts at 30, 14 and 7 days routed to the owner. Shorter-lived certs force automation. Track it as an operational metric.

topics.name: Senior Scenarios
topics.blurb: Design and 'what would you do' questions

concepts.what: Use the same four steps every time.
concepts.why: Nobody expects a perfect design. They're watching how you think.
concepts.ex:
1. Clarify    users, uptime target, data, budget, deadline
2. Propose    the simple version first, draw the boxes
3. Trade-offs what you'd change at more scale or less budget
4. Operate    monitoring, backups, rollback, runbook
concepts.tip: Ask one or two clarifying questions before answering. It shows seniority.

qa.q: Design the infrastructure for a new internal web app used by 2,000 employees.
qa.a: Clarify uptime, data sensitivity and peak load. Then: two web VMs behind an L7 load balancer with health checks and TLS termination, app tier separate from the database, database with replication and backups, an internal DNS name, firewall rules per tier, monitoring on the golden signals and host metrics, central logs, cert expiry alerts, a patch group, and a runbook. Trade-offs: VMs vs containers, shared vs dedicated database.

qa.q: Migrate 150 machines to a new OS or platform. How?
qa.a: Inventory first: hardware, apps, dependencies, owners. Pilot with 5–10. Automated builds so every machine is identical. Waves by site and criticality, with rollback (keep the old image for two weeks). A validation checklist per machine, a communication plan, and metrics per wave. If you've done one, tell it with your own numbers.

qa.q: The app is slow and three teams are blaming each other. What do you do?
qa.a: Get data before opinions. Check LB latency per backend (is it one server?), server CPU, memory and disk I/O, app logs for slow calls, database wait stats, and the network path. Build a timeline of what changed. Narrow it down by elimination and share findings with evidence, not blame.

qa.q: 40 certificates across LBs, web servers and apps are about to expire. Plan?
qa.a: Inventory every cert and expiry date. Group by renewal method: internal CA, public CA, ACME. Automate what you can. Schedule the rest in change windows by expiry date. Add monitoring at 30, 14 and 7 days so it never sneaks up again.

qa.q: You inherit a critical server with no documentation. How do you take it over?
qa.a: Back it up first. Inventory OS, packages, running services, listening ports, cron jobs, mounts, and who connects to it (LB pools, DNS records, firewall rules). Read configs and logs. Write the doc as you go and change nothing until you understand the dependencies.

qa.q: How would you cut server build time from 4 hours to 30 minutes?
qa.a: A golden image or template, automated install (cloud-init, Ubuntu autoinstall, Kickstart, or sysprep with unattend), Ansible for post-build configuration, a request form that feeds the automation, and a validation script that checks the standard. Measure before and after.

qa.q: High availability vs disaster recovery vs fault tolerance?
qa.a: Fault tolerance: no interruption at all (redundant power supplies, RAID). High availability: automatic recovery in seconds to minutes (LB pools, cluster failover). Disaster recovery: recovery at another site after a major event, within a planned RTO and RPO.

qa.q: What would you do in your first 90 days?
qa.a: First 30 days: learn the environment, read runbooks, shadow on-call, meet app owners, map what is and isn't monitored. Next 30: pick the top two pain points, usually alert noise and manual builds, and fix one. By day 90: propose a roadmap with measurable targets and own a patch cycle end to end.

qa.q: Design DR for a tier-1 app running in one Azure region.
qa.a: Start with RTO/RPO from the business. Then: infra as code so the second region can be built or kept warm, data replication (SQL failover groups, GRS storage, ASR for VMs), global traffic routing (Front Door or Traffic Manager) with health-based failover, secrets and certs available in both regions, DNS and firewall rules pre-staged, and a tested runbook. Run a real failover test at least yearly; an untested DR plan is a guess.

qa.q: The business wants an app live in two weeks. Normal lead time is six. What do you do?
qa.a: Don't just say yes or no. Find what's truly needed for day one (MVP), run long-lead items in parallel (cert, firewall, DNS, CAB), use standard templates, and make the risks explicit in writing: what's skipped (load test, DR) and who accepts it. Get the business owner to sign the risk acceptance, and schedule the remaining work as follow-ups.

qa.q: How do you decide between building on VMs or moving an app to containers/PaaS?
qa.a: Ask: is the app stateless, is the vendor supporting containers, does the team have the skills to run them, what are the scaling and release-frequency needs, and what's the cost of running VMs (patching, hardening) vs a platform. Legacy, stateful or vendor-locked apps stay on VMs; new stateless services go to PaaS or containers. Say the trade-off out loud.

qa.q: Your team is drowning in manual tickets. How do you fix it?
qa.a: Measure first: categorize a month of tickets and find the top five types by volume and time. Automate or self-service the biggest (Ansible job, Terraform module, ServiceNow catalog item), fix root causes of repeat incidents, and track ticket volume before and after. Show the hours saved in numbers.
